## earnings — module synthesis

_Source: `earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md`_

# Earnings Module — AMZN (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Amazon's earnings are accelerating at the operating level: EBIT margin reached a record 13.1% in Q1 2026 and CFO has grown faster than revenue for three consecutive years, driven by an AWS cloud consumption surge (28% growth, fastest in 15 quarters) and advertising scaling at 22–24% with near-zero incremental cost. The biggest driver is the pace at which AWS revenue outpaces the depreciation charge accumulating from an annualized $170B gross capex program — a race between billing ramp and D&A that cannot be tracked quarterly because Amazon does not disclose quarterly D&A. The consensus bar is stretched on operating income: the Street sits at $23.4B for Q2 2026, at the 86th percentile of management's own $20–24B guidance range, discounting all three named cost headwinds. The biggest risk is that $131.8B in FY2025 capex and $43.2B in Q1 2026 alone begin flowing through the Technology and Infrastructure line faster than new AWS billings offset them — an asymmetric, opaque headwind carrying a Low confidence tag because the D&A schedule is not disclosed. The red-flag agent returned a **Critical concerns** verdict; earnings are accelerating on operating metrics but carry material structural opacity around GAAP EPS quality and D&A timing.

## 1. Earnings Verdict

- **Verdict:** Earnings accelerating
- **Earnings quality /100:** 75 — strong at the operating level (CFO/EBITDA 95%+, negative CCC, no aggressive accruals); reduced from a potential 80+ by recurring equity investment EPS noise, SBC exclusion from normalized figures, and the server useful-life flip-flop in consecutive years
- **Consensus setup /100 (higher = more beatable):** 38 — revenue bar is beatable (consensus $195.8B sits just below the guidance midpoint); operating income bar is stretched ($23.4B at the 86th percentile of management's range), and the post-Q1 EPS revision cycle (+12.4% in 90 days) has raised the bar sharply; no individual cap triggered but the asymmetric operating income setup warrants a sub-40 score
- **Earnings volatility /100 (higher = worse):** 42 — multi-year AWS contracts and $364B backlog (management commentary, unaudited) anchor earnings against most demand shocks; score reflects the D&A capex-wave asymmetry and advertising's semi-cyclical exposure
- **Next-quarter setup:** Balanced — revenue likely clears; operating income pivotal on AWS sustaining 28%+ growth and at least one of three named cost items (Leo, fuel, SBC step-up) landing at the low end of its range
- **Biggest earnings driver:** AWS revenue growth rate vs D&A accumulation from the AI infrastructure capex program — a 5-percentage-point change in AWS growth moves EBIT by approximately $3B at the current run rate
- **Biggest earnings risk:** D&A step-up from $131.8B FY2025 / $43.2B Q1 2026 capex entering the Technology and Infrastructure line faster than AWS billings can offset, compressing Q2–Q4 2026 EBIT margins below consensus with no observable advance warning because quarterly D&A is not disclosed; simultaneously, the Anthropic Level 3 mark-to-model asset ($60.6B) has injected ~$15.3B in non-operating gains into FY2025 reported EPS and ~$15B more in Q1 2026, making the EPS consensus baseline fragile
- **Red-flag agent overall severity verdict: Critical concerns** (2 critical, 14 high, 10 medium flags — 26 triggered total)

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation

**Strongest bear point:** The D&A from the AI capex wave is the single most dangerous and least visible risk. Gross capex ran at $43.2B in Q1 2026 alone; once spent, that depreciation is locked in and will flow through the Technology and Infrastructure line over 5–30 year asset lives regardless of how AWS revenue performs. T&I costs already rose 120 basis points of revenue in FY2025. If the Q4 2025 / Q1 2026 capex cohorts enter the depreciation schedule before the corresponding customer billing begins (management explicitly disclosed a 6–24 month lag), EBIT could compress materially and invisibly — analysts cannot track it quarterly because Amazon does not break out D&A from T&I in the 10-Q.

**Strongest bull point:** The $364B AWS backlog (a 49% jump in a single quarter), combined with management statements that supply — not demand — is the binding constraint, suggests the revenue ramp will outpace D&A if data center installation and billing proceed on the stated timeline. Fulfillment operating leverage is also real and currently delivering: units growing 15% while fulfillment costs grew 9% and shipping costs grew 12% in Q1 2026.

**Single killer risk specific to earnings quality and the beat/miss setup:** The Q1 2026 normalized EPS beat of +69.5% drove a 12.4% upward revision to FY2026 consensus ($8.69), but that beat was materially amplified by Anthropic mark-to-model gains (~$15B booked in Q1 2026 per the 10-Q subsequent event). If Capital IQ's normalized EPS construct did not fully exclude this gain, the FY2026 EPS consensus is built on an inflated Q1 baseline. Every subsequent quarter would then print below run-rate on normalized EPS even on strong operating results — a systematic miss pattern manufactured by an accounting reclassification.

**Disconfirming evidence already visible:** AWS EBIT margin declined from 37.1% (FY2024) to 35.4% (FY2025) — precisely the D&A-overtaking-revenue dynamic — even though Q1 2026 recovered to 37.7%. Strict FCF is negative LTM (−$2.5B) while EBITDA accelerates, confirming the capex wave is real, not theoretical. The operating income consensus sits at the 86th percentile of management's own guidance range, meaning the Street has already partially ignored the risks management named; these are not tail risks, they are named, quantified line items.

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| Specialist | Verdict Line | Biggest Finding |
|---|---|---|
| earnings-data-triage | Sufficient — all required data categories present; only minor gap is absence of standalone spot price | Full Capital IQ estimates workbook current as of 2026-06-26; FY2025 10-K + Q1 2026 10-Q + four consecutive quarterly transcripts all available |
| historical-financials | Revenue re-accelerated to +16.6% YoY in Q1 2026; EBIT margin hit record 13.1%; strict FCF turned negative (−$2.5B LTM) on AI capex surge | EBIT margin expanded from 2.6% (FY2022 trough) to 13.1% (Q1 2026) — a ~1,050 bps recovery; CFO grew faster than revenue in FY2023, FY2024, and FY2025 |
| revenue-drivers | AWS consumption and AI workloads are the single most consequential revenue driver; FX-neutral Q1 2026 organic growth was 15%, not 17% | AWS backlog jumped from $244B to $364B in one quarter; advertising grew 22–24% for three consecutive quarters at near-zero marginal cost |
| margin-drivers | AWS revenue growth pace vs D&A accumulation from the AI capex wave is the single biggest margin driver | T&I costs rose from 13.9% to 15.1% of revenue in FY2025; one-time FY2025 charges ($4.6B) absent in FY2026 creates a ~60 bps base-effect tailwind |
| guidance-consensus | Bar is high on operating income ($23.4B consensus at 86th percentile of guidance range); revenue bar is beatable | FY2026 EPS consensus revised up +12.4% in 90 days post Q1 beat; all metrics rising over 90-day window; most recent revision 2026-06-26 |
| beat-miss-setup | Setup is balanced — revenue likely clears; operating income is the pivotal variable | Beat requires AWS sustaining 28%+ and cost headwinds at the low end simultaneously; miss requires only two of three named cost items (Leo ~$1B, fuel ~$1B, SBC seasonal step-up) to land high |
| earnings-quality | Quality score 75/100 — strong at the operating level; penalized for equity investment EPS noise, SBC exclusion, and server useful-life changes | CFO/EBITDA 95%+ for three consecutive years; reported EPS inflated by $2.47/share from $15.3B Anthropic/Rivian gains in FY2025 |
| earnings-sensitivity | Earnings volatility score 42/100 (higher = worse); D&A from AI capex wave is the #1 sensitivity variable with highest absolute EBIT impact and lowest confidence | D&A bear case (T&I rate +200 bps) = ~$5.7B EBIT headwind; AWS growth and D&A are correlated adversely — both driven by the same capex program |
| earnings-red-flags | **Critical concerns** — 2 critical, 14 high, 10 medium, 26 flags total | Critical flags: (1) Anthropic $60.6B Level 3 mark-to-model asset already injected ~$15B in Q1 2026 GAAP/possibly normalized EPS; (2) D&A from AI capex wave is the #1 risk, asymmetrically dangerous, and cannot be modeled from disclosed quarterly data |

## 3. Reconciliation

**Disagreement 1: Guidance-consensus vs beat-miss-setup on bar assessment.** Agent 04 calls the bar "high"; agent 05 calls the setup "balanced." Both are correct within their scope and at different levels of abstraction. Agent 04 is describing the operating income bar specifically (consensus at 86th percentile of guidance range — genuinely high). Agent 05 is describing the full Q2 2026 setup across all metrics, where the revenue bar is easy, making the total picture balanced rather than clearly biased toward a miss. Both agents agree on the underlying numbers. **Reconciled view:** The setup is balanced overall, with an explicitly stretched operating income bar. The synthesis carries both descriptions: "Balanced — revenue bar easy, operating income bar stretched."

**Disagreement 2: Earnings-quality score vs business-model red-flags-sweep on GAAP earnings reliability.** Agent 06 assigns a 75/100 quality score, correctly characterizing operating-level quality as high. The business-model red-flags-sweep adds the Anthropic correlated-risk dimension (correlated commercial and financial exposure) and notes GAAP net income is "partially fictitious at the headline level." The two agents are not in conflict on source data — they are assessing different layers of the earnings stack. **Reconciled view (conservative):** Operating income quality is high (75+); GAAP net income quality is medium (60–68) because equity investment swings have been material in 4 of the last 5 years. This synthesis reflects the distinction explicitly.

**Disagreement 3: Red-flag agent surfaced Critical concerns from the red-flag scan; the historical-financials and revenue-drivers agents describe the setup more constructively.** These agents are not contradicting each other — they are analyzing different time horizons and different metrics. Historical-financials and revenue-drivers describe a real acceleration in operating income and revenue. The red-flag agent identifies risks around how that acceleration is reported (EPS quality) and risks to its sustainability (D&A timing). **Reconciled view:** Both are correct. The earnings acceleration verdict is maintained, but the red-flag agent's Critical concerns verdict is reported verbatim and reflected in the caveats throughout.

No material disagreements on any numerical fact across specialists. All agents use the same underlying source files and their figures are mutually consistent.

## 4. Score Cap Application

| Cap Trigger | Applied? (Y/N) | Affected Score | Final Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| No consensus / estimate data | N — full Capital IQ estimates workbook present; most recent revision 2026-06-26 | Consensus setup | No cap triggered; max 30 cap does not apply |
| No cash flow statement | N — cash flow statement present in Capital IQ export (LTM through Mar-31-2026) and filings | Earnings quality | No cap triggered; max 45 cap does not apply |
| No revision history | N — Trends tab and Revisions tab both present; revision breadth (analyst-level up/down counts) unavailable but aggregate revision history is present | Consensus setup | Partial: revision breadth unavailable triggers max 60 cap; final consensus setup score of 38 is below 60, so the cap does not bind but is noted |
| Only inferred sensitivities | Partial Y — D&A/capex sensitivity confidence is Low (Inference); other sensitivities are Medium or High | Earnings volatility confidence | Applied: overall sensitivity confidence is Low for the #1 variable; earnings volatility confidence labeled Low for the D&A driver specifically |

**Note on the revision breadth cap:** The max-60 cap for "no revision history" does not apply because aggregate revision history is present; the cap that applies is for the specific absence of analyst-level up/down breadth counts, which triggers the max-60 variant on revision data quality. The final consensus setup score of 38 is well below 60, so this cap has no binding effect on the reported score but is disclosed for completeness.

## 5. Earnings Setup Summary

### Revenue Setup

The current revenue trajectory is sustainable at a 13–16% pace but not fully organic at the Q1 2026 reported rate of 17%. Approximately 1.8 percentage points of Q1 2026 revenue growth came from a favorable FX translation ($2.9B tailwind); management guided Q2 2026 FX to a near-neutral 10 basis points headwind, meaning the true organic engine is running at 15% and the reported rate will step down sequentially even if underlying demand holds. The single factor that would flip revenue direction is AWS growth decelerating from 28% toward 20% — either from a capacity installation delay or a macro-driven enterprise IT budget freeze. There is no material M&A, FX-restatement, or accounting reclassification inflating the revenue line (FY2025 acquisitions were explicitly immaterial per 10-K Note 5); the growth is organic. The reported FY2025 revenue of $716.9B and the Q1 2026 LTM of $742.8B both reflect genuine consumption-driven expansion across retail and cloud.

### Margin Setup

Current margins are NOT at a normalized run-rate; they are best described as a post-trough recovery still in progress. The FY2022 EBIT trough of 2.6% was caused by over-investment in fulfillment and a Rivian loss — both non-structural. The recovery to 13.1% in Q1 2026 is real and largely company-driven (AWS mix shift, fulfillment efficiency, advertising leverage). Whether 13%+ is sustainable through the next cycle depends on a single question: can AWS revenue growth (currently 28%) outpace the D&A ramp from the $131.8B FY2025 / $43.2B Q1 2026 capex program? If T&I cost rates continue rising by 100–200 basis points per year as new capacity enters the depreciation schedule, EBIT margins will compress from today's record level even as AWS revenue grows — and management does not disclose quarterly D&A, making this invisible until a quarter prints. The segment with the most structural margin-protection is AWS itself, where Trainium chip adoption is expected to provide "several hundred basis points of operating margin advantage" at scale (CEO, Q1 2026 call) — but this is 2–4 years from realization. The company has no contractual cost pass-through in retail; Amazon absorbs input cost increases and passes them to 3P sellers via FBA surcharges, with a 1–2 quarter lag.

### Quality Check

The largest gap between reported and economic earnings is the systematic inclusion of large equity investment marks in GAAP net income: $15.3B in FY2025 gains (Anthropic reclassification + Rivian) inflated reported EPS from a normalized $4.70 to $7.17 — a $2.47/share or 34% inflation. This pattern recurred in FY2021 (+$14.7B), FY2022 (−$15.9B), and FY2025 (+$15.3B), and a further ~$15B was booked in Q1 2026 per the 10-Q subsequent event. The gap is widening as Amazon's strategic investment portfolio grows, particularly the Anthropic position ($60.6B Level 3). The recurring baseline "Other operating expense" of $700–800M per year (before the FY2025 spike to $4.6B) is labeled as non-recurring every year — it is not. For modeling normalized earnings, this synthesis recommends starting from operating income (EBIT) rather than GAAP net income or normalized EPS, because EBIT is unaffected by investment gains, is the metric management guides to, and is the only earnings line that was directly disclosed with guidance. If using EPS, use normalized EPS ($8.69 FY2026 consensus) but apply a SBC haircut (approximately $1.80/share at current run rate) to arrive at true economic earnings — reducing the effective bar to approximately $7.00 on a fully-loaded basis.

### Consensus Bar

For the bar to be beaten materially on operating income in Q2 2026, AWS would need to sustain at or above 28% revenue growth while all three named cost headwinds (Leo ~$1B, fuel ~$1B, SBC seasonal step-up of unknown magnitude) land at the low end simultaneously — a set of conditions that must be true together. The revenue bar, by contrast, is set just below the guidance midpoint ($195.8B consensus vs $196.5B midpoint) and Amazon has beaten revenue consensus in all four of the most recently reported quarters by 1.0%–3.5%. The consensus is most likely set incorrectly on the high side for operating income: the $23.4B number embeds record AWS momentum continuing and zero adverse cost realization from three items management explicitly warned about. The most anchored piece of the current consensus is the FY2026 revenue estimate ($823.4B, a 14.9% growth assumption), which is defensible given the AWS backlog and advertising trajectory. The operating income consensus ($103.8B for FY2026) is less defensible if the T&I cost rate continues rising. A meaningful fraction of the current Q2 2026 revenue beat expectation is also tied to the Prime Day pull-forward into Q2 — an event-driven lift that compresses the Q3 comparison.

## 5b. Leverage & Capital Structure

**Trigger assessment:**
- Net Debt / Adjusted EBITDA (broad basis, includes lease liabilities): $55,518M ÷ $145,731M = **0.38x** at FY2025 year-end — below the 3.0x threshold for Trigger A.
- YoY change: broad-basis net debt moved from $54,199M (FY2024) to $55,518M (FY2025) = +$1,319M absolute increase, or +2.4% — below the 50% threshold. Net debt / EBITDA: 0.45x (FY2024) → 0.38x (FY2025), a decline of 0.07x — below the 1.0x change threshold for Trigger B.
- At the LTM March 2026 level, broad-basis net debt rose to $92,451M (a +70.6% increase from FY2024 year-end $54,199M), driven by a sharp increase in reported long-term debt ($73.4B at Dec-31-2025 to $127.3B at Mar-31-2026, likely reflecting new debt issuance in Q1 2026). However, on a strict basis (financial debt only, no leases), Amazon held net cash of approximately $12.5B at March 31, 2026. The broad-basis LTM jump reflects the lease liability inclusion methodology, not a true leverage deterioration; the strict basis moved from net cash of $46.1B at FY2025 year-end to net cash of $12.5B at Q1 2026-end, a material reduction in the net cash cushion but not a net-debt position.

Neither Trigger A nor Trigger B fires on the criteria as written (annual basis comparison), though the LTM Q1 2026 broad-basis change warrants watching. Leverage is within normal range and did not change materially during the annual period — no dedicated treatment required.

## 6. Key Numbers

- **Revenue growth rate:** +12.4% FY2025; +16.6% YoY Q1 2026 (FX-neutral: +15%) [FY2025 10-K, p.24; Q1 2026 10-Q]
- **EBITDA margin:** 20.3% FY2025; EBIT margin 11.2% FY2025, 13.1% Q1 2026 (record) [Capital IQ Income Statement; Q1 2026 10-Q]
- **EPS (normalized):** $4.70 FY2025 (Capital IQ Normalized); $2.78 Q1 2026; $8.69 FY2026 consensus; note: reported EPS $7.17 FY2025 includes $15.3B in Anthropic/Rivian gains [Capital IQ Estimates — Consensus tab; FY2025 10-K]
- **CFO / EBITDA:** 95.7% FY2025; 95.3% LTM Mar-31-2026 [Capital IQ Cash Flow; Section 1 bridge]
- **Biggest driver current level:** AWS revenue $37.6B in Q1 2026 (+28% YoY); backlog $364B (management commentary, unaudited); advertising $17.2B Q1 2026 (+24% YoY) [Q1 2026 transcript; Q1 2026 10-Q]
- **Consensus gap (Q2 2026):** Revenue: consensus $195.8B vs guidance midpoint $196.5B = −$0.7B (consensus below midpoint); Operating income: consensus $23.4B vs guidance midpoint $22.0B = +$1.4B (consensus at 86th percentile of range) [Capital IQ Estimates — Trends tab, as of 2026-06-26]
- **Estimate revision direction:** All metrics rising over the 90-day window; FY2026 EPS consensus +12.4% in 90 days post Q1 beat; revision pace decelerating over the most recent 30 days [Capital IQ Estimates — Trends tab]
- **Earnings volatility score:** 42/100 (higher = worse) [07_earnings-sensitivity, Section 7]

## 7. What Would Change The Earnings Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Upgrade It | What Would Downgrade It | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Earnings accelerating | AWS growth rate accelerating beyond 30% for two consecutive quarters, demonstrating that new capacity is being billed faster than the D&A ramp; Trainium chip savings materializing earlier than the 2–4 year management timeline; strict FCF returning to positive as the capex cycle peaks | T&I cost rate rising a further 150+ basis points in H2 2026, signaling D&A growth is outpacing AWS revenue growth; Amazon printing Q2 2026 operating income near the guidance floor ($20–21B) against the $23.4B consensus; a tariff escalation causing measurable reduction in China-seller GMV and advertising spend; AWS EBIT margin settling at 35–36% rather than recovering toward 38%+ | Q2 2026 results (July 31, 2026): AWS revenue growth rate vs Q1 2026's 28%; T&I cost as a percentage of Q2 revenue (the proxy for D&A ramp since quarterly D&A is not disclosed); Q3 2026 operating income guidance; confirmation from Capital IQ that Q1 2026 normalized EPS of $2.78 excludes Anthropic-related gains; first audited RPO disclosure for the AWS backlog |

## 8. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Dominant earnings trend:** Operating earnings are genuinely accelerating — EBIT grew from $13.3B (FY2022) to $80.0B (FY2025) to an LTM rate of $85.4B, and Q1 2026 operating margin of 13.1% is the highest in Amazon's history. The driver is not one thing but a convergence: AWS growing at 28%, advertising growing at 22%+, fulfillment costs growing slower than units, and the absence of FY2025 one-time charges ($4.6B) creating a YoY base-effect tailwind in FY2026.

- **Earnings quality: split verdict.** Operating income quality is high — CFO/EBITDA at 95%+ for three years, negative cash conversion cycle, no accrual fraud signals. GAAP net income quality is medium: equity investment swings ($15.3B in FY2025, $14.7B in FY2021, −$15.9B in FY2022) make reported EPS structurally unreliable as an earnings trend indicator. Normalized EPS is the right metric but the Q1 2026 normalized EPS of $2.78 may itself contain Anthropic mark-to-model gains that Capital IQ has not separately stripped — this has not been confirmed and is the most consequential quality uncertainty for the FY2026 consensus.

- **Consensus bar:** Revenue bar is beatable (consensus sits just below the guidance midpoint and Amazon has beaten revenue in all four of the most recently reported quarters). Operating income bar is stretched — the $23.4B consensus for Q2 2026 requires everything going right simultaneously. For FY2026, the EBIT consensus of $103.8B implies a T&I cost rate holding at or below current levels; if T&I continues rising, the FY2026 EBIT consensus could be 5–10% too high.

- **Next-quarter setup and Q3 look-ahead:** Q2 2026 is balanced. Q3 2026 looks structurally cleaner: the SBC step-up is Q2-specific, Leo costs begin partial capitalization in Q4, and Prime Day will have already been recognized in Q2 (removing it as a Q3 variable). The D&A risk does not diminish in Q3 — it compounds.

- **Red-flag agent severity verdict (verbatim): Critical concerns.** 2 critical flags, 14 high flags, 10 medium flags, 26 triggered total. This must be conveyed to the master synthesizer without softening. The two critical flags are: (1) Anthropic Level 3 investment ($60.6B, mark-to-model) — already injected ~$15.3B into FY2025 GAAP EPS and ~$15B into Q1 2026; GAAP and possibly normalized EPS are unreliable measures of operating performance and create correlated risk (the most important AWS customer relationship is simultaneously a $60B equity-like holding that would impair alongside any AWS demand slowdown); (2) D&A from AI capex wave — the primary thesis risk is asymmetrically dangerous to the downside, opaque in the quarterly income statement, and cannot be modeled from disclosed data.

- **Top sensitivity variable:** The D&A / T&I cost rate step-up from the AI capex wave. It is the variable with the largest absolute EBIT impact in the sensitivity table (~$7.1B average swing) and the only sensitivity variable classified with Low confidence because the D&A schedule is not disclosed quarterly. Management explicitly described a 6–24 month lag from capex spending to customer billing — meaning the $43.2B spent in Q1 2026 will produce depreciation before it produces AWS revenue in a number of cases.

- **Partial-data cap:** The only partial-data limitation is the absence of analyst-level revision breadth (broker identity gated in Capital IQ export). This triggers the max-60 cap on consensus setup, but the final score of 38 is below 60, so the cap does not bind. No other caps apply. The Q1 2026 normalized EPS attribution (whether Capital IQ's $2.78 excludes the Anthropic subsequent-event gain) is the biggest missing data point — this is not a data-availability gap but a data-quality verification need that could change the entire EPS consensus picture.

- **Biggest missing data point:** Audited quarterly D&A disclosure (Amazon does not break out D&A from T&I in the 10-Q) — this is the single data point that would most improve the quality of the forward earnings model and allow the D&A/capex timing risk to be tracked. Second: audited RPO table confirming the $364B AWS backlog composition (committed contracts vs indicative pipeline).

- **What would change the earnings verdict:** An operating income print near $20–21B for Q2 2026 (vs $23.4B consensus) alongside a weak Q3 guidance would flip the verdict to "Earnings decelerating." AWS growth accelerating beyond 30% for two consecutive quarters with stable T&I cost rates would upgrade the verdict to a cleaner "Earnings accelerating" with higher conviction. The current verdict is warranted but the confidence level is medium, not high, because the primary risk variable (D&A timing) is opaque in quarterly disclosures.

- **Thesis type note (CLAUDE.md §14):** The master synthesizer should be aware that this is partly a "sector-cycle / capex-cycle" thesis, not purely company-specific. The question of whether Q2–Q4 2026 beats or misses consensus is dominated by D&A timing on a $170B-annualized capex program — a capital expenditure cycle bet — not by product innovation or market share dynamics. CLAUDE.md §24 filter 3 (high debt and survival test) does not directly apply given Amazon's net cash position on a strict basis, but the FCF compression (strict FCF −$2.5B LTM) and the AI capex commitment create a cash-allocation dependency that the master synthesizer should register.

## 9. Simple Summary

- Revenue growing 13–16% organically, led by AWS (28% YoY in Q1 2026) and advertising (22%+); FX added 1.8 pp to Q1 reported growth that will not repeat in Q2
- EBIT margin at record 13.1% in Q1 2026, expanding from a 2022 trough of 2.6%; expansion driven by AWS mix shift, fulfillment efficiency gains, and advertising leverage — but T&I costs are rising faster than revenue as the AI capex wave depreciation begins
- Earnings are not fully clean at the GAAP level: $15.3B equity investment gain (Anthropic/Rivian) inflated FY2025 reported EPS by $2.47/share; operating income quality is genuinely high (CFO/EBITDA 95%+) but GAAP headline earnings are structurally noisy
- Consensus bar on revenue is beatable; operating income bar ($23.4B for Q2 2026 = 86th percentile of management's $20–24B range) is stretched and requires near-perfect execution on three simultaneously uncertain cost items
- Next-quarter setup is balanced: revenue beat likely, operating income beat requires AWS sustaining 28%+ growth; miss requires only two of three named cost headwinds to land at the high end
- Biggest sensitivity variable: D&A step-up from the AI capex wave — $43.2B in Q1 2026 alone is locking in future depreciation that cannot be tracked quarterly; asymmetric downside; Low confidence tag
- Earnings volatility score: 42/100 (higher = worse) — material but not extreme, anchored by AWS multi-year contracts and negative cash conversion cycle
- This module is highly useful for the master synthesizer: it establishes that the earnings acceleration is real and operating-level quality is high, but that the GAAP EPS line is unreliable, the consensus bar is stretched on the most important metric, and the primary risk to the thesis is invisible in quarterly disclosures — a combination that makes the setup more fragile than it appears on a headline metrics basis

# Historical Financials — AMZN

**Reporting standard:** US GAAP. **Currency:** USD (millions unless noted). **Fiscal year end:** December 31. **Listing:** Nasdaq Global Select Market. **Primary filing regime:** US SEC (10-K / 10-Q).

**FCF definitions used in this report:**
- *Company-disclosed FCF* (non-GAAP, as defined in the 10-K): CFO minus purchases of property and equipment net of proceeds from sales and incentives.
- *Strict FCF* (this report's cross-module standard): CFO minus total capex as reported in the cash flow statement (gross, before proceeds).
- Both are shown where they differ materially. The company's own FCF is the lead figure for trend analysis because management explicitly tracks it.

**Net debt basis note:** Two bases are shown throughout.
- *Strict basis* (financial debt only, excluding lease liabilities): total financial debt (short-term borrowings + current portion of long-term debt + long-term debt) minus cash and short-term investments. At FY2025 year-end this yields a net cash position of approximately $46.1B.
- *Broad basis* (Capital IQ definition, includes operating and finance lease liabilities in debt): used for the Net Debt / EBITDA ratio shown in the annual table and where labeled. At FY2025 year-end this is $55,518M.
The broad basis is used for leverage tracking because Amazon's lease obligations are economically debt-like. Both bases are labeled in every table.

## 4. Reported vs Adjusted Metrics

Amazon does not formally report non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA or adjusted EBIT. The company does report one non-GAAP measure officially: *Free Cash Flow* (defined in the 10-K, p.28). Capital IQ constructs a "Normalized" EPS series by removing investment gains and losses; this is a vendor construct, not company-disclosed.

Special charges in Q3 and Q4 2025 are the only in-period adjustments relevant to EBIT; management called them out but did not publish a formal "adjusted operating income" line.

| Metric | Reported Value (FY2025) | Adjusted / Normalized Value | Adjustment Amount | Adjustment Reason | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| EPS diluted | $7.17 | $4.70 (normalized) | −$2.47/share | Removes $15,301M gain on equity investments (primarily Anthropic mark-to-market reclassification and Rivian) included in "Other income" | [3] Capital IQ Income Statement, FY2025 — "Gain on Sale of Invest." $15,301M; FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.27 (Other Income/(Expense) description) |
| EBIT (Operating Income) | $79,975M | ~$84,275M (one-time-adjusted) | +$4,300M | Removes Q3 2025 special charges: $2.5B FTC settlement + $1.8B severance costs | [6] Q3 2025 Earnings Call transcript, Oct 30, 2025; FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.27 "Other operating expense (income), net was $763M and $4.6B in 2024 and 2025" |
| EBITDA | $145,731M | No company-adjusted figure disclosed | N/A | Company does not disclose adjusted EBITDA | FY2025 10-K — no adjusted EBITDA table |
| FCF (company-disclosed) | $11,194M | N/A — this is already the company's own non-GAAP figure | N/A | Definition: CFO minus PP&E net of proceeds/incentives; differs from strict CFO-minus-gross-capex ($7,695M) because it nets $3,499M in asset sale proceeds against capex | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.28 (Free Cash Flow reconciliation table) |

**EPS note:** The FY2025 reported EPS of $7.17 is inflated by $15,301M in "Gain on Sale of Investments" — primarily reclassification adjustments on Amazon's investment in Anthropic (from available-for-sale debt to nonvoting preferred stock) and observable price changes on Rivian shares. This is not recurring operating income. The normalized diluted EPS of $4.70 (a Capital IQ construct, not a company-issued figure) is more representative of operating earnings power. Analysts and the beat/miss surprise data track normalized EPS. The annual table uses reported EPS; normalized EPS is the relevant series for trend analysis of underlying earnings.

**FY2022 anomaly:** Reported EPS was −$0.27 in FY2022, driven by a $15,926M *loss* on equity investments (Rivian's share price collapse), not from operating losses. Operating income (EBIT) in FY2022 was $13,348M (positive but depressed by cost pressures). Normalized EPS in FY2022 was $0.68. This explains why reported EPS is volatile while operating income trends are more informative.

Revenue share percentages for FY2023 are estimated from year-over-year growth rates in earnings transcripts because quarterly FY2023 figures are not directly disclosed in the data pool on a standalone basis. FY2024 and FY2025 shares use audited annual totals plus quarterly data from filings and transcripts. FY2023 estimates are labeled.

| Quarter | FY2023 Rev Share [est] | FY2024 Rev Share [est] | FY2025 Rev Share | Avg Rev Share | FY2023 EBITDA Mgn | FY2024 EBITDA Mgn | FY2025 EBITDA Mgn |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 | ~19.9% | ~20.9% | 21.7% | ~20.8% | Annual only: 14.9% | Annual only: 19.0% | Annual only: 20.3% |
| Q2 | ~23.3% | ~23.5% | 23.4% | ~23.4% | See note | See note | See note |
| Q3 | ~25.0% | ~25.2% | 25.1% | ~25.1% | See note | See note | See note |
| Q4 | ~31.9% | ~30.4% | 29.8% | ~30.7% | See note | See note | See note |

**EBITDA margin note:** Only annual EBITDA is available from the data pool. Quarterly D&A is not disclosed in the 10-Q income statement. Intra-year EBITDA margin estimates have been omitted rather than computed from approximated D&A, to avoid presenting unreliable inferences as facts.

**Key seasonality finding:** Q4 consistently accounts for approximately 30–32% of annual revenue — materially above the 25% that a flat-distribution quarter would represent. The 10-K explicitly confirms Q4 as the seasonally heavy quarter. Q4 2025 at 29.8% is the lightest Q4 share in this three-year window, likely reflecting the continuing shift of Prime Day from Q3 to Q2/Q3, and faster-growing AWS revenue (which has no holiday seasonality and grows year-round), diluting the retail Q4 spike as a share of the total.

Q1 is consistently the lightest quarter (~20–22% of annual revenue). The Q1-to-Q4 gap is approximately 8–10 percentage points, making Q4 the dominant revenue and (inferably) cash-generation quarter.

No quarter takes less than 19% or more than 32% of annual revenue, so the thresholds for flagging extreme seasonality (>30% or <20%) are approached but not breached except Q4 in FY2023 (31.9%) and FY2024 (30.4% — just over the 30% threshold).

**Flag:** Q4 consistently takes >30% of annual revenue (FY2023 and FY2024 clearly; FY2025 at 29.8% just below). This represents meaningful concentration: roughly one-third of Amazon's retail revenue falls in the November–December holiday window.

## 6. Key Trend Summary

**Revenue direction — Stable, with Q1 2026 re-accelerating.** Revenue growth has held in a narrow 9–12% band for five years (FY2021–FY2025), with FY2025 at +12.4% being the top of that range. Q1 2026 printed +16.6% year-over-year — the fastest quarterly growth in several years — driven by AWS accelerating to 28% and retail segments posting double-digit gains. Whether the acceleration sustains or Q1 2026 is an outlier (partly aided by FX tailwinds of $2.9B) is the central question for the forward period.

**Margins — Expanding sharply, recovering from a 2022 trough.** The FY2022 EBIT margin of 2.6% was a multi-year low caused by over-investment in fulfillment capacity during COVID, a Rivian investment loss, and cost inflation. The recovery since then has been consistent and steep: EBIT margin went from 2.6% (FY2022) to 6.4% (FY2023) to 10.8% (FY2024) to 11.2% (FY2025) to a record 13.1% in Q1 2026. Gross margin has expanded 830 basis points from FY2021 to FY2025, driven by mix shift toward high-margin AWS and advertising. The margin expansion trend is the most important development in the financials over this five-year window.

**Seasonality — Material, Q4-concentrated.** Approximately 30% of annual revenue lands in Q4, creating meaningful quarterly volatility in reported earnings and cash flow. AWS partially offsets this because cloud demand is not holiday-driven, but the retail segments (combined 82% of revenue) carry the seasonal shape. Investors and analysts should treat Q4 as the earnings anchor quarter and Q1 as the seasonal trough.

**Inflection points.** Two clear inflection points over this period: (1) FY2022 — an operating losses-adjacent period (positive EBIT but depressed; negative reported EPS from Rivian) from which Amazon has recovered strongly; and (2) the FY2025–2026 capex surge driven by AI investment in AWS. The AI-driven capex step-up (gross capex rose from $83B in FY2024 to $132B in FY2025 to $43B in a single quarter in Q1 2026) is compressing FCF materially in the near term — strict FCF went from +$32.9B (FY2024) to +$7.7B (FY2025) to a negative LTM position of −$2.5B. This is intentional and management has framed it as investing ahead of confirmed customer demand (AWS backlog of $364B as of Q1 2026), but it is a genuine FCF inflection point that the rest of this module should treat as structural for 2025–2027.

# Revenue Drivers — AMZN

**Reporting standard:** US GAAP. **Currency:** USD (millions unless stated). **Fiscal year end:** December 31. **Listing:** Nasdaq. **Date of analysis:** 2026-07-03. **Most recent quarter:** Q1 2026 (ended March 31, 2026).

---

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Segment decomposition applied — 3 segments from business-model module: North America (59% of FY2025 revenue), International (23%), and AWS (18%). Each segment has a materially different revenue driver profile. The business-model segment-map (analyses/AMZN_2026-07-03/business-model/03_segment-map.md) was read and applied. The external-dependency module (10_external-dependency.md) was also read and applied to the cycle-position assessment.

Amazon does not disclose a cyclicality classification for AWS or Advertising within the segment filing. However, the business-model external-dependency module classifies the overall company as "Partly externally driven" with a score of 32/100, driven primarily by regulatory, tariff, and consumer-cycle exposure in the retail segments. AWS is treated as low-cyclical (multi-year contracts, sticky workloads). This is consistent with the MD&A and transcript evidence.

**Cycle-position read (Cycle-Position Rule):** Amazon is not a commodity, auto, or capital-goods company and does not follow a classical commodity price cycle. However, the AWS cloud-adoption cycle is relevant. Current AWS growth of 28% year-over-year in Q1 2026 — the fastest in 15 quarters — reflects the early-to-mid stage of an AI-driven enterprise cloud adoption cycle, not a peak. Evidence: CEO Andy Jassy stated at the Q1 2026 call that "We've never seen a technology grow as rapidly as AI" and explicitly drew the analogy to the first AWS growth wave, saying "we're in the early stages." This is not a run-rate peak; it is an adoption ramp. The retail segments are mid-cycle on consumer spending, with no peak signal visible in Q1 2026 unit growth of 15% year-over-year. No one-time policy or macro tailwind has been identified in the most recent results that would make the current growth non-run-rate, except Q1 2026 FX which added $2.9B (approximately 1.8 percentage points) to the reported 17% revenue growth; the FX-neutral growth rate was 15%. The FX tailwind is flagged as a reversal risk for subsequent quarters.

---

## 2. Revenue Driver Tree

Amazon is a multi-segment business. The correct formula is:

**Total Revenue = (NA Retail: Online + Physical + 3P Services + Subscriptions + Advertising) + (International: same lines + FX) + (AWS: Cloud customers × consumption per customer × price per unit)**

At a product-type level (from Note 10, FY2025 10-K, p.69):

| Product / Service Type | FY2023 Revenue ($M) | FY2024 Revenue ($M) | FY2025 Revenue ($M) | FY2025 Share | YoY Growth |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Online stores | $231,872 | $247,029 | $269,287 | 37.6% | +9.0% |
| Physical stores | $20,030 | $21,215 | $22,561 | 3.1% | +6.3% |
| Third-party seller services | $140,053 | $156,146 | $172,162 | 24.0% | +10.3% |
| Advertising services | $46,906 | $56,214 | $68,635 | 9.6% | +22.1% |
| Subscription services | $40,209 | $44,374 | $49,619 | 6.9% | +11.8% |
| AWS | $90,757 | $107,556 | $128,725 | 18.0% | +19.7% |
| Other | $4,958 | $5,425 | $5,935 | 0.8% | +9.4% |
| **Consolidated** | **$574,785** | **$637,959** | **$716,924** | **100%** | **+12.3%** |

**Source:** FY2025 10-K, Note 10, p.69 (filed April 9, 2026).

**Company-specific revenue formula (one line):**
> Revenue = (Online store GMV × net revenue rate) + (Physical store throughput) + (3P GMV × commission rate) + (Advertising impressions × CPM) + (Prime members × subscription fee) + (AWS cloud consumption × blended price/unit)

## 3. Market / Share / Price / Mix Split

| Driver Bucket | Current Direction | Evidence | Importance /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|

**Key separation:** Retail volume growth (units) is company-execution driven (selection, price, delivery speed); it outpaces apparent consumer-spending GDP growth, suggesting share gain. AWS growth is both market-demand driven (AI adoption structural wave) and share-driven (enterprise workload transitions). Price/realization is a deliberate mix of slight retail price reduction and AWS contract-driven pricing headwinds. None of the revenue growth requires attribution to M&A or accounting reclassification.

## 6. Revenue Growth Decomposition

**Most recent annual period: FY2025 vs. FY2024**

Total revenue: $716,924M (FY2025) vs. $637,959M (FY2024) = +$78,965M = +12.4% growth.

The 10-K explicitly discloses FX effect and segment growth rates. Volume vs. price split is disclosed qualitatively in MD&A but not in a single precise table. The decomposition below uses the disclosed FX table (p.29), segment growth rates (p.24), and the product-type revenue table (Note 10, p.69). Where individual components cannot be precisely split, the basis is labeled.

|---|---:|---|

Net pricing effect is slightly negative on a blended basis. [FY2025 10-K, p.24; Q1 2026 transcript, CEO: "average prices...decreased vs. prior year"] — Inference, not a directly disclosed line item |

**Most recent quarter (Q1 2026 vs. Q1 2025):**

Q1 2026 revenue: $181,519M vs. Q1 2025: $155,667M = +$25,852M = +16.6%.

| Component | Contribution to Growth (pp) | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| FX translation | ~+1.8 pp | CFO stated "$2.9B favorable FX impact"; $2.9B / $155,667M = +1.9 pp [Q1 2026 transcript, CFO] |
| AWS volume acceleration | ~+2.5 pp (incremental vs. FY2025 run rate) | AWS grew 28% in Q1 2026 vs. 20% in FY2025; AWS ~18% weight; faster AWS growth contributed incremental ~2.5 pp lift [Q1 2026 transcript, CFO: "$37.6B and growth accelerated 480 bps to 28%"] |

**Q1 2026 note:** Excluding the $2.9B FX tailwind, organic growth was approximately 15% — above the FY2025 12.4% rate. This represents genuine acceleration, not solely an FX effect. However, Q1 2026 FX should be treated as a one-time tailwind because Q2 2026 guidance implies a near-neutral (10 basis points) FX impact going forward, per CFO guidance. The underlying organic 15% growth rate — not 17% — is the better run-rate estimate for Q2+ comparisons.

## 7. The Single Biggest Revenue Driver

**AWS consumption volume, including AI-driven workloads, is the single driver that would most move Amazon's revenue if it changed by 10–20%.**

AWS represents $128.7B of FY2025 revenue and is growing at 28% annually. A 20% change in AWS's growth rate (from 28% to 34%, or from 28% to 22%) would shift incremental AWS revenue by approximately $7–8B per year. That is only the direct revenue effect. Because AWS runs at a 35.4% EBIT margin — versus 7% in North America and 2.9% in International — a 10% swing in AWS revenue has nearly four times the profit impact of an equivalent retail swing. AWS is already the dominant driver of consolidated operating income (57% of the total from 18% of revenue), so any acceleration or deceleration in AWS growth rate has a disproportionate effect on group profitability.

**Current direction:** Accelerating. Q1 2026 AWS growth of 28% year-over-year is the fastest in 15 quarters and is being driven by two concurrent forces — the ongoing enterprise migration of on-premises workloads to the cloud, and the new and structurally larger wave of generative AI workloads. The $364B revenue backlog (up 49% from $244B just one quarter earlier) means AWS has committed future revenue across multi-year customer contracts well in excess of two years of current run-rate revenue. The binding constraint is supply (data center capacity), not demand. Management is investing $43.2B in a single quarter to bring more capacity online.

**The risk to this direction** is a capacity timing mismatch: if new data center capacity (which takes 6–24 months from cash outlay to customer billing per management disclosure) comes online slower than expected, or if a global recession causes enterprise IT budget freezes before these contracted workloads scale, AWS growth would slow. This is the most consequential single variable for Amazon's revenue trajectory over the next 12–18 months.

## earnings / 03_margin-drivers.md

_Source: `earnings/03_margin-drivers.md`_

# Margin Drivers — AMZN

**Reporting standard:** US GAAP. **Currency:** USD (millions unless noted). **Fiscal year end:** December 31. **Latest annual period:** FY2025 (10-K filed April 9, 2026). **Latest quarter:** Q1 2026 (10-Q filed April 30, 2026).

**Sector overlay applied: Multi-sided platform and cloud infrastructure conglomerate — margin analysis uses a hybrid grammar.** AWS (18% of revenue, 57% of operating income) uses SaaS/cloud metrics: GAAP gross margin, technology-and-infrastructure cost rate, operating leverage, SBC as % of revenue. The Stores segments (North America + International, 82% of revenue, 43% of operating income) use retail/generic operating company metrics: cost of sales rate, fulfillment cost rate, SG&A leverage. Advertising and subscriptions (embedded in the Stores segments) are high-margin service lines tracked at the operating income level. No single SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md row applies cleanly; the two dominant grammars (SaaS/cloud for AWS; retail/generic for Stores) are applied side by side throughout this report.

**Cycle-position read:** Amazon's current margin level is NOT a normalized run-rate. The FY2022 EBIT margin of 2.6% was a trough caused by over-investment in fulfillment capacity and a Rivian loss. The recovery since then has been steep and largely company-driven (mix shift to AWS, fulfillment network regionalization, advertising scale). The Q1 2026 EBIT margin of 13.1% is, per the CFO, "our highest operating margin ever." This is best read as a post-trough recovery that is not yet at a long-run ceiling — AWS margins are still expanding and the Stores segments still have meaningful operating leverage to extract. The primary cycle risk is not a demand downturn but a capex overshoot: gross capex of $43.2B in Q1 2026 alone ($173B annualized pace) means FCF is deeply negative on a strict basis and will remain so for 2–3 years unless AWS revenue growth accelerates faster than capex. This is an intentional investment cycle, not a cyclical demand cycle. No policy tailwind is embedded in the current margin (the 2025 Tax Act benefited cash taxes, not GAAP EBIT).

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Amazon reports three segments with disclosed operating income per segment. Segment-level EBITDA and segment-level free cash flow are NOT disclosed. Gross margin is disclosed only at the consolidated level (and in the 10-Q income statement). The segment breakdown used throughout this report is:

| Segment | FY2025 Revenue | Revenue Share | FY2025 Operating Income | Operating Income Share | EBIT Margin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| North America | $426,305M | 59% | $29,619M | 37% | 7.0% |
| International | $161,894M | 23% | $4,750M | 6% | 2.9% |
| AWS | $128,725M | 18% | $45,606M | 57% | 35.4% |
| Consolidated | $716,924M | 100% | $79,975M | 100% | 11.2% |

Sources: FY2025 10-K, Note 10 — Segment Information, p.67, filed April 9, 2026.

This is a clearly multi-segment business where segment mix is the single most important margin driver. Decomposition is performed for all three segments below.

## 2. Cost Stack

Amazon's disclosed operating expense lines from the FY2025 10-K (Item 7, p.25) are used directly. The generic COGS/freight/SGA/R&D split is adapted to Amazon's actual disclosed lines, which differ from a standard manufacturing cost stack.

**AWS costs are primarily classified under "Technology and infrastructure" — not under cost of sales.** The 10-K states explicitly: "Costs to operate our AWS segment are primarily classified as 'Technology and infrastructure.'" This means the cost of sales line reflects retail/fulfillment costs, and the technology-and-infrastructure line carries the majority of AWS's operating cost base.

| Cost Line | FY2024 Amount | FY2024 % of Revenue | FY2025 Amount | FY2025 % of Revenue | YoY Change | Direction | Evidence | Margin Risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| Cost of sales (retail product + shipping + digital content) | $326,288M | 51.1% | $356,414M | 49.7% | +9% | Improving (declining as % of revenue) | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.25 | Low-Mid — shipping costs growing but at slower rate than revenue; $102.7B shipping in FY2025 vs $95.8B FY2024 |
| Fulfillment (operating fulfillment centers, physical stores, customer service, payment processing) | $98,505M | 15.4% | $109,074M | 15.2% | +11% | Stable (flat as % of revenue) | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.25 | Mid — unit growth outpacing cost growth in Q1 2026 (units +15%, fulfillment cost +9% YoY) |
| Technology and infrastructure (AWS + R&D + data centers + D&A on servers) | $88,544M | 13.9% | $108,521M | 15.1% | +23% | Worsening (rising as % of revenue) | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.25 | High — primary cost of the AI capex wave; D&A on new data centers flows through here with a 6–24 month lag |
| Sales and marketing | $43,907M | 6.9% | $47,129M | 6.6% | +7% | Improving (leverage being extracted) | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.25 | Low — growing slower than revenue; advertising revenue ($56B+ annualized) offsets some of this structurally |
| General and administrative | $11,359M | 1.8% | $11,172M | 1.6% | −2% | Improving (declining as % of revenue) | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.25 | Low — 10-K states G&A "did not significantly change" in 2025 vs 2024 |
| Other operating expense (income), net (incl. FTC settlement, severance, impairments) | $763M | 0.1% | $4,639M | 0.6% | +508% | One-time (FTC $2.5B + severance $1.8B in Q3 2025) | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.25; Q3 2025 Earnings Call, Oct 30, 2025 | Low on a run-rate basis — these were one-time charges; run-rate "other" is ~$763M (FY2024 level) |
| SBC (stock-based compensation, embedded in above lines) | $22,018M | 3.5% | $19,531M | 2.7% | −11% | Improving | Capital IQ Income Statement export, FY2025; FY2025 10-K | Low — SBC declining as % of revenue; not a GAAP separate line but embedded; 2.7% is moderate for a tech company |
| Shipping costs (subset of cost of sales) | $95,800M | 15.0% | $102,700M | 14.3% | +7% | Improving (declining as % of revenue) | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.25 MD&A Cost of Sales section | Mid — fuel inflation flagged for Q2 2026; partially offset by FBA surcharge on 3P sellers |
| D&A (embedded in technology and infrastructure) | Not separately disclosed for the annual period | — | Not separately disclosed | — | Accelerating (inference from capex growth) | FY2025 10-K — D&A not broken out from T&I | High — the primary mechanism by which current capex ($131.8B gross FY2025; $43.2B in Q1 2026 alone) flows into the P&L over 5–30 year useful lives |

**Pass-through dynamics:** Amazon does not use contractual cost-escalation clauses on retail. Input cost increases (shipping, wages, energy) are absorbed first and then offset through scale and efficiency. In Q1 2026, CFO Olsavsky noted fuel cost increases were "partially offset by the recently implemented fuel and logistics-related FBA surcharge" — meaning part of the fuel cost increase was passed to third-party sellers via higher FBA fees, not to end consumers. Pass-through lag for shipping/fuel costs is approximately 1–2 quarters based on management commentary. AWS unit prices decline over time (long-term customer contracts include price concessions), so on the AWS side there is no cost pass-through mechanism — the offset is volume outrunning unit price declines. [Q1 2026 Earnings Call, CFO prepared remarks, April 29, 2026; FY2025 10-K, MD&A Cost of Sales, p.25]

## 3. Gross Margin → EBITDA Margin → EBIT Margin Walk

| Margin Level | FY2024 | FY2025 | Change (bps) | Q1 2025 | Q1 2026 | YoY Change Q1 (bps) | Main Reason | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Gross margin | 48.9% | 50.3% | +140 bps | 50.6% | 51.8% | +120 bps | Mix shift: AWS (classified under T&I, not COGS) and advertising growing faster than 1P retail; shipping cost growing slower than revenue | FY2025 10-K, p.25 (cost of sales 51.1%→49.7%); Q1 2026 10-Q income statement |
| EBITDA margin | 19.0% | 20.3% | +130 bps | Not available by quarter | Not available by quarter | Not available | Gross margin expansion partially offset by T&I cost growth (+23% YoY in FY2025) which includes D&A step-up from prior capex waves | Capital IQ Income Statement, FY2024/FY2025 |
| EBIT margin (operating margin) | 10.8% | 11.2% | +40 bps | 11.8% | 13.1% | +130 bps | AWS segment margin expansion + North America continuing to recover; partially offset by $4.6B in one-time charges (FTC settlement, severance, impairments) in FY2025 | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.27; Q1 2026 Earnings Call, CFO remarks |

**FX note:** In FY2025, foreign exchange rates reduced net sales by $4.4B and reduced operating expenses by $4.1B, for a net $358M adverse impact on reported operating income. In Q1 2026, FX was a $2.9B tailwind to revenue (CFO stated 15% constant-currency growth vs 17% reported). The FX impact on operating income is not separately disclosed for Q1 2026 but the Q1 2026 10-Q transcript states "we expect [FX] to be a headwind of approximately 10 basis points" for Q2 2026. [FY2025 10-K, Item 7, FX effect table, p.29; Q1 2026 Earnings Call, CFO guidance remarks]

**AWS operating margin context (sector overlay):** AWS EBIT margin was 35.4% in FY2025 ($45,606M on $128,725M revenue), up from 37.1% in FY2024 ($39,834M on $107,556M revenue). The decline of ~170 bps YoY reflects the step-up in technology-and-infrastructure spending (the primary AWS cost). In Q1 2026, AWS operating income was $14,161M on $37,600M revenue = 37.7% margin, indicating sequential improvement as new capacity comes online and efficiency gains on existing capacity accelerate. CEO Andy Jassy stated in the Q4 2025 call that Trainium chips are expected to provide "several hundred basis points of operating margin advantage versus relying on others' chips for inference" at scale. [FY2025 10-K, Note 10, p.67; Q1 2026 10-Q, Note 8; Q4 2025 Earnings Call, Feb 5, 2026; Q1 2026 Earnings Call, Apr 29, 2026]

**Pass-through lag (input costs to margin):** Price increases for shipping/fuel passed to 3P sellers (via FBA surcharge) lag input cost increases by approximately 1 quarter based on the Q1 2026 call timing (surcharge implemented in Q1 after fuel costs rose). AWS D&A on new data center capacity has a 6–24 month lag from when capex is spent to when it hits the P&L, per CEO commentary ("AWS has to lay out cash for land, power, buildings, chips, servers and networking gear in advance of when we can monetize it, typically 6 to 24 months before we start billing customers"). [Q1 2026 Earnings Call, CEO prepared remarks]

## 4. Margin Walk — Which Margin Level Matters Most?

**EBIT margin (operating margin) is the primary margin metric for Amazon**, and specifically the segment-level EBIT margin for AWS vs the Stores segments. Here is why.

Amazon does not separately disclose segment EBITDA. The consolidated gross margin is distorted by the accounting classification: AWS costs run through "Technology and infrastructure," not "Cost of sales," so gross margin understates AWS's true gross economics and overstates the retail gross margin relative to what a standalone retailer would show. Using gross margin to track Amazon would give a false read on whether the margin expansion is structural (mix shift to AWS) or cyclical (retail efficiency gains).

EBIT margin captures the full cost structure including the critical T&I line that carries AWS costs. It is the level at which segment operating income is disclosed. It is also what management guides to (Q2 2026 guidance is for operating income of "$20–24 billion," not gross profit or EBITDA).

EBITDA margin is relevant for understanding the FCF bridge (EBITDA minus capex approximates the investment intensity), but it is not the primary driver metric because Amazon's D&A is economically meaningful — unlike a REIT where D&A is non-economic, Amazon's data centers and fulfillment infrastructure do depreciate, and the current capex wave will produce real D&A growth over the next 3–5 years.

For the retail segments specifically, gross margin and fulfillment cost rate are useful sub-metrics for tracking network efficiency (e.g., fulfillment cost as % of revenue went from 15.4% to 15.2% YoY — a sign of leverage). But the consolidated primary metric is EBIT margin.

| FX | −50 bps | −50 bps | Net FX impact on operating income was −$358M [FY2025 10-K, FX table, p.29] |
| Total reported EBIT margin change | +40 bps (from 10.8% to 11.2%) | ~+430 bps (on-time-adjusted) | FY2025 10-K, consolidated operating income $68,593M→$79,975M |

**Interpretation:** The true operating improvement in FY2025 (stripping out one-time charges) was approximately 400–430 bps. The reported gain of only 40 bps dramatically understates the underlying progress. In FY2026, the absence of the one-time charges is itself a ~60 bps tailwind to EBIT margin on a full-year basis.

The Q1 2026 vs Q1 2025 bridge shows an even cleaner picture: operating margin expanded 130 bps year-on-year (11.8%→13.1%) with no material one-time items, driven by fulfillment efficiency, AWS revenue acceleration, and advertising growth.

---

## 8. The Single Biggest Margin Driver

**The pace at which AWS revenue growth outpaces D&A from the AI infrastructure capex wave is the single largest margin driver for the next 12–24 months.**

Here is the logic. Amazon is spending at an annualized rate of approximately $170B in gross capex as of Q1 2026, almost entirely for AWS data centers, chips, and power. This capex converts into D&A (flowing through "Technology and infrastructure") over 5–30 years. The immediate effect is that T&I costs rose 23% in FY2025 while total revenue rose only 12% — a 120 bps drag on consolidated EBIT margin from this line alone. This drag will continue and likely worsen in 2026 as Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 capex enters the depreciation schedule.

The only offset is AWS revenue growth. If AWS accelerates from 28% (Q1 2026 rate) toward a higher rate as more capacity comes online and the $364B backlog converts to billings, the revenue can outrun the D&A. If AWS growth decelerates — whether from a demand slowdown, a hyperscaler market-share shift, or a competitor pricing event — D&A continues to grow while revenue slows, and consolidated EBIT margin compresses materially. A 500 bps deceleration in AWS revenue growth (e.g., 28%→23%) at the current run rate would reduce AWS revenue growth by approximately $3B per quarter at Q1 2026 scale, which at AWS's ~37% EBIT margin represents roughly $1B of EBIT at risk per quarter — or approximately 55 bps of consolidated EBIT margin on an annualized basis.

The current direction of this driver is mixed: AWS growth is accelerating (28% in Q1 2026, up from 24% in Q4 2025, the fastest growth in 15 quarters), which is positive. But capex is also accelerating, management has committed to continued heavy investment through at least 2027, and the D&A tail will be long. The Trainium chip cost savings (described as "several hundred bps of operating margin advantage" at scale) are the structural offset — but they are 2–4 years from full realization. Until then, the AWS revenue growth rate is the single variable that most determines whether consolidated margins expand or compress.

Four-quarter summary: Revenue beat every quarter by 1.0%–3.5%. EPS beat three of four quarters, with Q4 2025 in-line and the other three registering very large beats (25%–69%). This pattern suggests the consensus bar has been set below what Amazon actually delivers on earnings, particularly for EPS, while the revenue bar has been more accurately calibrated.

The Q1 2026 EPS beat (+69.5%) was unusually large. A beat of this magnitude is typically partly explained by tax timing, mark-to-market gains (Rivian / other equity holdings), or one-time items in addition to operating strength. Without a full earnings quality breakdown, calling this fully recurring would be premature — that is the domain of the `06_earnings-quality` agent.

## 7. Bar Assessment

**Bar is high** — consensus is above guidance midpoint on operating income and sits at elevated post-Q1-beat levels; estimates have been raised sharply (EPS FY2026 +12.4% in 90 days) and the absolute miss on operating income would require delivering only toward the bottom of the guidance range.

**Rationale:** Management guided Q2 2026 operating income to $20–24B, a wide $4B range. The Street's EBIT consensus sits at $23.4B, at the 86th percentile of that range. This means the Street is effectively betting against the downside risks management explicitly named (Leo launch costs ~$1B, fuel inflation, SBC step-up). If any of those costs come in at the high end of the range, operating income printing near $20–21B would register as a miss against a $23.4B consensus.

On revenue, the bar is more fairly set: consensus of $195.8B sits just below the guidance midpoint of $196.5B (gap of −$0.7B, or −0.4%), which means a print anywhere within the guidance range would register as a beat against the Street number. The revenue bar is therefore beatable.

The asymmetry between a tight revenue bar and a stretched operating income bar is the key setup heading into Q2 2026 results (scheduled July 31, 2026). Amazon has beaten on revenue consistently but the EPS bar has been moved sharply higher after the Q1 print, and the wide guidance range on operating income gives management more room to disappoint than the consensus implies.

## 1. Next Quarter Context

The next print is Q2 2026, scheduled for approximately July 31, 2026. Q2 is a seasonally mid-weight quarter — historically accounting for approximately 23–24% of annual revenue versus Q4's 30%+ — with a notable wrinkle: management explicitly stated Q2 2026 guidance assumes Prime Day falls in Q2 in most major geographies (including the US), which is a shift from the traditional Q3 timing. That assumption makes Q2 2026 tougher than a typical Q2 because any shortfall in Prime Day lift would fall directly on the quarter. The consensus bar for operating income is stretched: the Street sits at $23.4B EBIT, at the 86th percentile of management's own $20–24B guidance range, implying analysts are largely discounting the downside risks management explicitly named. Revenue consensus of $195.8B sits just below the guidance midpoint of $196.5B, making the revenue bar comparatively easier to clear. ## 6. Seasonality Read

Q2 is historically a mid-weight quarter for Amazon, accounting for approximately 23–24% of annual revenue — the second-lightest quarter after Q1 (21–22%). Critically, Q2 2026 is non-standard: management's guidance explicitly assumes Prime Day occurs in Q2 2026 for the US and most large geographies, shifting an event that was Q3 in recent years into Q2. This compresses the typical Q2-to-Q3 step-up (Prime Day effect) and makes Q2 a harder quarter to miss on revenue, but also a harder quarter to meaningfully beat because the Prime Day lift is already embedded in the $194–199B guidance range. Seasonality is neither a pure tailwind nor headwind for Q2 2026 — the Prime Day pull-forward is the dominant calendar effect, and it cuts both ways: it gives the quarter an event-driven demand catalyst but also raises the expected revenue bar relative to a normalized Q2. EBIT margins in Q2 typically benefit from the Prime Day advertising surge (sellers paying for visibility) but are partially offset by the SBC step-up that management explicitly flagged. [Sources: FY2025 10-K, Item 1 p.4, seasonality disclosure; 01_historical-financials, Section 5; Q1 2026 Earnings Call, CFO prepared remarks]

---

## 7. Historical Pattern

Amazon has beaten consensus revenue estimates in all four of the most recently reported quarters, by margins of 1.0%–3.5%. EPS beats have been even larger — 25–70% in three of the four quarters — suggesting the consensus EPS bar has been systematically set too low relative to what Amazon has been delivering on the operating income and operating margin line. However, the Q1 2026 EPS beat of +69.5% was partly driven by non-recurring items (Anthropic mark-to-market reclassification) that inflated reported EPS well above operating earnings power, so the streak of large EPS beats may overstate the underlying consistency of the operating beat pattern. Revenue beats have been more modestly consistent, in a 1–3.5% range, with no revenue miss in at least four quarters. The synthesizer should weight the revenue beat pattern moderately — it is real, but the magnitude has varied — and should be cautious about over-weighting the large EPS beats given their partly non-recurring nature in recent quarters. The key post-Q1 shift is that the EPS consensus bar has now been raised sharply (+12.4% for FY2026 EPS in 90 days), so the degree of difficulty for a repeat EPS beat is higher. [Capital IQ Estimates, Surprise tab; 04_guidance-consensus, Sections 6 and 7]

---

## 8. Setup Verdict

**Setup is balanced.**

The weight of evidence does not cleanly favor a beat or a miss. Revenue is likely to clear the Street number — the consensus of $195.8B sits just below the guidance midpoint and the historical beat pattern on revenue is consistent. The pivotal uncertainty is operating income: consensus at $23.4B assumes all the management-flagged cost headwinds (Leo ~$1B, fuel ~$1B, SBC step-up) land at the low end of their range while AWS continues its Q1 momentum. If even two of those three cost items land at the high end, a miss on operating income against the $23.4B consensus is the more likely outcome even on a clean revenue beat.

**The single most important factor in the verdict is whether AWS revenue growth sustains at or above 28% in Q2 2026.** AWS at 28% growth would provide sufficient incremental high-margin revenue to absorb the cost headwinds and print operating income near $23–24B; AWS decelerating even modestly (to 24–25%) would leave the cost headwinds uncompensated and print near the guidance midpoint of $22B, a ~$1.4B miss against consensus.

**The single biggest risk that could flip the verdict in either direction:** On the upside, an early read suggesting Q2 2026 AWS exited the quarter above 30% growth (supply constraints easing as new capacity comes online) would decisively favor a beat. On the downside, a tariff escalation on Chinese-origin goods between now and the July 31 print — specifically one that causes Chinese sellers to materially reduce advertising spend on the platform — could compound the operating income miss risk by suppressing the one line (advertising) that is both the fastest-growing and the highest-margin.

---

## 9. Second-Quarter Look-Ahead

Q3 2026 looks structurally better than Q2 on two dimensions. First, some of the one-time cost headwinds embedded in Q2 (Leo pre-launch expense, SBC step-up) should moderate — management stated Leo costs will begin partial capitalization in Q4, and the SBC step-up is an annual Q2 event, not a Q3 recurrence. Second, Q3 is seasonally a revenue ramp quarter, historically capturing ~25% of annual revenue versus Q2's ~23%, and the Prime Day effect will have already been recognized in Q2, making the Q3 revenue comparison cleaner. The risk to this more constructive Q3 view is D&A: each additional quarter of $40–45B capex adds to the depreciation base, and the T&I cost line (which carries AWS D&A) will continue rising as a percentage of revenue unless AWS growth accelerates further to offset it.

---

## 10. Pre-Mortem

If this setup fails — specifically, if Amazon misses Q2 2026 operating income against consensus — the most likely reason we misjudged it would be an underestimation of the pace at which the AI capex wave's depreciation flows through the T&I line. The analysis correctly identifies D&A from the AWS build as the primary margin risk, but the exact timing of when new assets enter the depreciation schedule is not disclosed and requires inference from the 6–24 month capex-to-billing lag the CEO cited. If depreciation accelerates faster than new AWS revenue begins billing, the T&I line expansion compounds the known one-time cost headwinds and the combined impact pushes operating income toward the bottom of the guidance range — a scenario the consensus has not priced. The secondary miss driver would be a larger-than-expected tariff impact on 3P seller advertising spend, which would be difficult to observe in advance and would have compressed the quarter's highest-margin revenue line.

# Earnings Quality — AMZN

**Reporting standard:** US GAAP. **Currency:** USD (millions unless noted). **Fiscal year end:** December 31. **Sources:** FY2025 10-K (filed Apr 9, 2026); Q1 2026 Form 10-Q (filed Apr 30, 2026); Capital IQ Financials export (Cash Flow, Balance Sheet, Income Statement, Ratios tabs, data as of Apr 30, 2026); Q1–Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 earnings call transcripts.

---

## 1. EBITDA → CFO → FCF Bridge (5 years + LTM)

Capex split between maintenance and growth is not disclosed by Amazon. Total gross capex from the cash flow statement is used throughout. The company's own FCF definition (CFO minus capex net of property sale proceeds and incentives) is shown alongside the strict definition (CFO minus gross capex). Note: *"Capex split not disclosed — total capex used. Strict FCF may understate true recurring free cash flow because Amazon's disclosed FCF nets out $3.5B in asset sale proceeds in FY2025."*

All figures USD millions.

| Item | FY2021 | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | LTM Mar-26 | Trend |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| EBITDA | 59,312 | 55,269 | 85,515 | 121,388 | 145,731 | 155,861 | Accelerating |
| Working capital change (net) | (13,716) | (21,086) | (17,318) | (18,541) | (19,319) | (26,542) | Deteriorating |
| Tax paid | (3,688) | (6,035) | (11,179) | (12,308) | (8,295) | (8,741) | Volatile |
| Interest paid | (1,772) | (2,142) | (3,112) | (2,364) | (1,949) | (2,039) | Improving |
| SBC and other non-cash | 5,191 | 20,746 | 31,040 | 27,302 | 23,346 | 29,953 | Stable |
| **CFO** | **46,327** | **46,752** | **84,946** | **115,877** | **139,514** | **148,531** | Accelerating |
| Capex (gross, total) | (61,053) | (63,645) | (52,729) | (82,999) | (131,819) | (151,003) | Accelerating (surge) |
| Asset sale proceeds | 5,657 | 5,324 | 4,596 | 5,341 | 3,499 | 3,704 | Stable |
| **FCF — strict (CFO − gross capex)** | **(14,726)** | **(16,893)** | **32,217** | **32,878** | **7,695** | **(2,472)** | Deteriorating |
| **FCF — company disclosed (CFO − net capex)** | N/A | N/A | N/A | 38,219 | 11,194 | N/A | Decelerating |
| **CFO / EBITDA %** | **78.1%** | **84.6%** | **99.3%** | **95.5%** | **95.7%** | **95.3%** | Strong / Stable |

**Working capital change** = sum of changes in accounts receivable, inventory, accounts payable, unearned revenue, and other net operating assets per Capital IQ Cash Flow tab.

**FCF normalisation note:** The FY2025 strict FCF of $7,695M and LTM FCF of −$2,472M reflect a deliberate, management-confirmed AI infrastructure investment surge: gross capex rose from $83B in FY2024 to $132B in FY2025 and $151B annualised at LTM Mar-26. Management explicitly framed this as investing ahead of confirmed demand (AWS backlog of $364B as of Q1 2026) and stated the pattern mirrors prior AWS build cycles that produced substantial downstream FCF. The near-term FCF compression is therefore a real cash drain but is a management-chosen reinvestment cycle, not an operating-quality defect. No single non-recurring cash item inflates the FCF figures — the company's own disclosed FCF ($11,194M for FY2025) is modestly higher than strict FCF because it nets out $3,499M in asset sale proceeds. The lead FCF figure used throughout this report is the **normalised operating FCF = CFO minus gross capex (strict)**, which is the most conservative measure. The company-defined FCF is shown alongside it, labelled.

[Sources: Capital IQ Cash Flow tab, FY2021–FY2025; FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.28 (FCF reconciliation); Q1 2026 Form 10-Q, Cash Flow Statement; Q4 2025 Earnings Call transcript (Feb 5, 2026)]

---

## 2. Cash Conversion Assessment

CFO/EBITDA has been above 78% in every year since FY2021 and above 95% in every year since FY2023. This is a genuinely high-quality cash conversion rate — it means that almost every dollar of EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, and the non-cash depreciation charge) turns into real operating cash. The consistency since FY2023 (99.3%, 95.5%, 95.7%) is notable given the scale of the business and the mix shift toward AWS, which carries high EBITDA margins and minimal working capital requirements. The near-term FCF compression is entirely a capex story, not a CFO story: operating cash generation is accelerating alongside EBITDA. CFO grew 20% in FY2025 and 28% year-over-year in LTM Mar-26. The one watch point is that working capital changes have been a consistent drag of $13–27B per year, driven by rapid receivables growth as AWS and third-party seller volumes scale; this is explored in Section 3.

---

## 3. Working Capital Trends

Metrics computed from Capital IQ Balance Sheet and Income Statement tabs (annual end-of-period). DSO uses total accounts receivable ÷ (revenue/365); DIO uses inventory ÷ (COGS/365); DPO uses accounts payable ÷ (COGS/365). Capital IQ Ratios tab used as cross-check (DSO 17.5–26.0, DIO 37.1–43.7, DPO 98.1–109.5, CCC −42.8 to −33.3 over FY2021–FY2025 — consistent with my calculations using the same end-of-period convention).

| Metric | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Direction | Risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Receivable days (DSO) | 27.1 | 26.3 | 28.7 | Rising | Low |
| Inventory days (DIO) | 39.9 | 38.3 | 39.2 | Stable | Low |
| Payable days (DPO) | 101.8 | 105.6 | 124.8 | Rising sharply | Medium (supplier signal) |
| Cash conversion cycle (DSO + DIO − DPO) | −34.8 | −41.0 | −56.9 | Improving | Positive |

**Flag assessment:**

- **DSO:** Rose 9.1% year-over-year in FY2025 (26.3 → 28.7 days), which is below the >10% trigger. The absolute level (28.7 days) is not elevated for a business of Amazon's mix — AWS billings and third-party seller fees carry longer settlement terms than retail. The Q1 2026 10-Q confirms customer receivables of $43.3B vs $40.4B at year-end, a modest sequential rise consistent with higher AWS run rate. No revenue recognition concern flagged. [Q1 2026 Form 10-Q, Note on Accounts Receivable]
- **DIO:** Rose 2.5% in FY2025 (38.3 → 39.2 days), below the >15% trigger. Inventory balance rose $4.1B (12% in dollar terms) against 9.2% COGS growth, a modest build. Capital IQ Ratios tab shows inventory turnover of 9.8x in FY2025 vs 9.7x in FY2024 — effectively flat. No channel stuffing signal.
- **DPO:** Rose sharply from 105.6 days (FY2024) to 124.8 days (FY2025), a +18.3% increase. This is the most notable working capital movement. At $121.9B, accounts payable grew faster than COGS ($121.9B vs $94.4B, implying about 40 days of extension in dollar terms). This is partly structural: Amazon's scale gives it strong negotiating leverage over suppliers, and the 10-K notes DPO variability driven by payment terms and supplier mix. However, an 18-point jump in a single year bears watching. It boosts near-term cash flow but signals potential supplier term extension.
- **CCC:** The cash conversion cycle is deeply negative at −56.9 days in FY2025, improving from −41.0 days in FY2024. A negative CCC means Amazon collects cash from customers before it must pay suppliers — an inherent structural advantage of its retail and marketplace model. The trend is improving, primarily driven by the DPO expansion.

## 4. Non-GAAP Adjustments

Amazon does not publish a formal "adjusted EBITDA" or "adjusted EBIT" table in its filings. The company's only official non-GAAP measure is Free Cash Flow, reconciled on 10-K p.28. Capital IQ constructs a Normalized EPS series (removing investment gains/losses). Management called out one-off charges in Q3 and Q4 2025 in transcripts but did not issue a formal adjusted operating income line.

| Adjustment | Amount | Recurring? (Y/N) | Concern Level | Evidence |

| Investment gain on equity securities (Anthropic reclassification + Rivian) in FY2025 "Other income" | +$15,301M pre-tax, +$2.47/share diluted EPS impact | N (mark-to-market / reclassification) — but has occurred in multiple years (FY2021 +$14.7B, FY2022 −$15.9B) | Mid — inflates FY2025 reported EPS significantly; normalized EPS $4.70 vs reported $7.17 | FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.27; Capital IQ Income Statement: "Gain on Sale of Invest." $15,301M |
| Stock-based compensation ($19,467M in FY2025) excluded from Capital IQ's Normalized EPS | $19,467M (2.7% of revenue) | Y — recurs every year; has never been below $12.8B in the last five years | Mid — SBC is real economic cost; excluding it consistently overstates adjusted earnings | FY2025 10-K, Note 4, p.53 (SBC expense table: $19,467M FY2025) |

| Server useful-life change (Jan 1, 2025: subset of servers/networking reverted from 6 to 5 years) | −$1,400M EBITDA impact (higher depreciation); −$1.0B net income; −$0.10/share diluted EPS | N — one-time accounting policy re-change | Low-Mid — actual impact is reduced earnings, not inflated; transparent disclosure | FY2025 10-K, Note 1, p.41 (lines 2471–2477) |
