## 3. Buyback Scorecard

| Year | Amount Spent | Currency | Shares Bought | Implied Avg Price | Share-Count Change (YoY, M shares) | Offset SBC Dilution? | Price-Discipline Evidence | Judgment | Source |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $0 | USD | 0 | N/A | +62M net dilution | No | $10B program not yet authorized | No buybacks | FY2023 10-K, Note 8 |
| FY2022 | $6,000 | USD | 46.2M | ~$129.87 | +141M net dilution despite buyback | No (141M net dilution = ~556M SBC-issued minus 46.2M repurchased) | Stock 52-wk range 2022: ~$102–$188 (post-split). Buybacks concentrated in H1 2022 before stock fell to $102 in Nov 2022. Bought at ~$130, near mid-range — not at the bottom. | Partial — buyback executed but at a sub-optimal price and did not reduce net share count | FY2024 10-K, Note 8; FY2023 10-K, Note 8 (Stock Repurchase Activity) |
| FY2023 | $0 | USD | 0 | N/A | +210M net dilution | No | $6.1B authorization unused; stock ranged ~$90–$153 (post-split; significant undervaluation by late 2022 / early 2023 standards) | No buybacks when arguably the best opportunity existed | FY2025 10-K, Note 8, p.62 |
| FY2024 | $0 | USD | 0 | N/A | +138M net dilution | No | $6.1B authorization unused; stock recovered $153–$225 | No buybacks as stock rerated | FY2025 10-K, Note 8, p.62 |
| FY2025 | $0 | USD | 0 | N/A | +23M net dilution | No | $6.1B authorization unused; stock $180–$244 | No buybacks; program fully dormant | FY2025 10-K, Note 8, p.62 |

**Key findings:**

1. **The $10B buyback program authorized in March 2022 has been 39% used (only $3.9B) in four years.** $6.1B remains unused as of December 31, 2025. [FY2025 10-K, Note 8, p.62]

2. **Buybacks never offset SBC dilution.** Shares outstanding rose from 10,242M (FY2021) to 10,754M (FY2025), a net increase of 512M shares (+5.0% over five years or ~+1.0%/year). RF-CAP-002 is triggered (buybacks not reducing share count). Gross SBC vesting over the period was approximately 558M shares; the $6B buyback offset only 46.2M of those shares in one year.

3. **Intrinsic-value discipline not fully assessable from this module** (valuation module has not run). However, on observable evidence: the $129.87/share average buyback price in FY2022 was not at the post-split trough (~$102 in late 2022). The company bought $6B before the stock fell and did nothing as the stock spent much of FY2023 well below the buyback price. This is not a pattern of patient, opportunistic repurchasing.

4. **Insiders sold into the dormant buyback period.** Jeff Bezos adopted a Rule 10b5-1 plan to sell up to 15M shares through February 2026; Andy Jassy adopted a plan to sell up to 142,224 shares through December 2026. The company was simultaneously sitting on $6.1B in unused buyback authorization. [FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74]

5. **Counterpoint:** Management's stated rationale for not buying back stock — that all capital should be reinvested in AWS/AI infrastructure — is internally consistent. The $131.8B capex in FY2025 dwarfs the $6.1B buyback authorization by 21x. The decision not to buy back shares is a defensible opportunity-cost trade-off (reinvest at 15–20% incremental ROIC rather than repurchase at a market multiple), but it does leave per-share value creation to organic earnings growth rather than share count reduction.

| Metric | FY2021 | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Payout ratio | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | FY2025 10-K, Item 5, p.19 |
| Dividend coverage (FCF) | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A | No dividend paid |
| FCF strict (CFO minus gross capex) | ($14,726)M | ($16,893)M | $32,217M | $32,878M | $7,695M | Capital IQ Cash Flow; FY2025 10-K, p.36 |
| Company-disclosed FCF | N/A | N/A | N/A | $38,219M | $11,194M | FY2025 10-K, p.28 (FCF reconciliation) |
| Gross capex / CFO | 131.8% | 136.1% | 62.1% | 71.6% | 94.5% | Computed: capex ÷ CFO by year |
| ROIC (NOPAT/avg invested capital, ~10% tax) | 17.2% | 6.9% | 15.1% | 20.1% | 18.1% | Computed (see below) |
| Incremental ROIC (ΔNOPAT/ΔIC) | N/A | (37.3%) | 34.6% | 24.8% | 15.9% | Computed (see below) |
| SBC as % of CFO | 27.5% | 41.9% | 28.3% | 19.0% | 13.9% | Capital IQ Supplemental; corroborated FY2025 10-K |

**ROIC computation methodology:**
- NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − 10%), using a conservative flat 10% tax rate (effective tax rates vary: ~7% FY2025, ~9% FY2024). The 10% rate is used as a through-cycle normalisation.
- Invested capital (IC) = total common equity + total financial debt (short-term borrowings + current LT debt + LT debt) − total cash and short-term investments. Lease obligations are excluded from financial debt (they are tracked separately via the broad net-debt basis).
- Beginning-of-year IC uses prior FY year-end balance sheet. FY2020 IC = $99,870M (equity $138,245M + fin. debt $57,674M − cash $96,049M).
- [Capital IQ Balance Sheet; FY2025 10-K, p.39 (Balance Sheet); FY2021 10-K Balance Sheet]

**Incremental ROIC detail:**

| Period | ΔNOPAT | ΔInvested Capital | Incremental ROIC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FY2021→FY2022 | ($10,378)M | +$27,789M | (37.3%) |
| FY2022→FY2023 | +$21,154M | +$61,050M | 34.6% |
| FY2023→FY2024 | +$28,567M | +$115,074M | 24.8% |
| FY2024→FY2025 | +$10,244M | +$64,378M | 15.9% |

**Interpretation:**
- FY2022 incremental ROIC was negative because Amazon significantly over-built fulfillment capacity during COVID and absorbed large equity investment losses from Rivian. This was a recognized misallocation year (EBIT fell from $24.9B to $13.3B on a $27.8B increase in invested capital).
- FY2023–FY2024 incremental ROIC of 35% and 25% respectively represents strong compounding evidence: each incremental dollar of capital deployed in those years generated well above the 9–10% estimated cost of capital.
- FY2025 incremental ROIC of 15.9% remains above cost of capital, but signals the initial wave of AWS/AI capex is compressing returns per-dollar-deployed. AWS segment capex jumped from $53.3B (FY2024) to $96.5B (FY2025), and the full revenue benefit of that spend is a 12–24 month lag.
- The FY2025 decline from 24.8% to 15.9% incremental ROIC is expected and not alarming — it reflects the front-loading of capex ahead of confirmed AWS backlog ($364B as of Q1 2026 per Q1 2026 Earnings Call, Apr 29, 2026). However, if FY2026–2027 incremental ROIC falls below 12%, the AWS investment thesis weakens materially.

**Balance-sheet prudence:**
- Net debt / EBITDA (broad basis, including leases): declining from 0.87x (FY2023) to 0.38x (FY2025). Strict net cash position at FY2025: ~$46.1B. [FY2025 10-K, p.39; Capital IQ Ratios]
- LTM Mar-31-2026 net debt (broad basis) rose to $92.5B, driven by $15.7B in new long-term debt issued November 2025 and further Q1 2026 debt issuance ($54B+ increment per Capital IQ). Strict basis at Mar-31-2026 is approximately net cash ~$12.6B (Q1 2026 10-Q balance sheet).
- Total contractual commitments: $439.7B as of Dec 31, 2025 — a very large off-balance-sheet obligation set, but all disclosed and asset-backed. [FY2025 10-K, Note 7, p.59]
- EBIT/interest coverage: 35.2x (FY2025). No solvency risk. [Capital IQ Ratios]

---

## 5. Capital-Allocation Read

Amazon's capital allocation over FY2021–FY2025 is **value-creative but with a clear flaw**: organic reinvestment in AWS and AI infrastructure is the dominant use (90.5% of CFO) and is generating returns (18–20% ROIC in FY2024–FY2025) that comfortably exceed the cost of capital; however, persistent SBC dilution (+5.0% net share count over five years) with a dormant buyback program means per-share value is created entirely through earnings power growth, not capital return. The best use of capital is unambiguously organic reinvestment — incremental ROIC of 25–35% in FY2023–FY2024 is exceptional by any standard. The worst use is the share-dilution-without-offsetting-buybacks dynamic: management sits on a $6.1B authorization while issuing equity-equivalent compensation at scale. M&A (MGM, One Medical) is bolt-on, rationally priced, and not the story — these are small deals relative to Amazon's scale. The single biggest capital-allocation signal is the $131.8B capex in FY2025 (a 3.1x capex-to-D&A ratio) guided to approximately $200B in FY2026: this is the largest organic capital bet in corporate history by dollar quantum, and the degree to which AWS backlog converts to revenue over the next 12–24 months will determine whether the incremental ROIC holds at 15%+ or collapses below cost of capital.

**Verdict: value-creative / disciplined**, with one ongoing blemish (share dilution not offset by buybacks).

# Incentives & Compensation — AMZN

**Reporting currency:** USD. **Fiscal year end:** December 31. **As of:** 2026-07-04.
**Jurisdiction:** US SEC (10-K, DEF 14A). **Partial-data cap applied:** Incentive alignment max 50/100 — the 2026 DEF 14A proxy statement (filed April 2026) is not in the data pool. Compensation structure and aggregate SBC are partially reconstructed from the FY2025 10-K, Capital IQ Takeover Defenses/Public Company Profile, and web-sourced information (labelled throughout).

## 1. Compensation Structure

| Executive | Base | Annual Bonus | Long-Term Incentive | Cash vs Equity Mix | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| CEO — Andrew R. (Andy) Jassy | $365,000 | $0 (none — no annual cash bonus for any NEO except new hires) | Time-vested RSUs from a 10-year grant made at CEO appointment (July 2021); 61,000 shares total granted, ~$212M fair value at grant; no new grant since 2021; vesting: 5%/15%/40%/40% in years 1–4, back-loaded; FY2025 SEC-disclosed total comp $2.07M (FY2024: $40.1M driven by RSU vesting; FY2025 $43M of unvested RSUs remain per 2026 proxy) | ~99.9% equity (of lifetime grant value); FY2025 "reported" total: $365K base + $0 new equity + $1.7M security/travel | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 (10b5-1 plan); Capital IQ Takeover Defenses (compensation philosophy); Web: 2026 DEF 14A filed Apr 8, 2026, as cited in Yahoo Finance Apr 2026 and salary.com (web-sourced, unverified) |
| CFO — Brian T. Olsavsky | $365,000 | $0 (same structure — no annual bonus) | RSU grants at intervals (not annually); most recent reported: 106,374 RSUs granted in 2026, vesting 2027–2032; FY2024 total comp ~$25.7M (RSU vesting year); FY2025 reported comp $372K (inter-grant year, no RSU vesting) | ~99% equity (in RSU vesting years); ~100% cash in inter-grant years | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 (10b5-1 plan termination Nov 2025); Web: StockTitan Form 4 filing (106,374 RSUs) and salary.com (web-sourced, unverified) |

**Notes on the table:**
- "Reported" total compensation in the 2026 proxy Summary Compensation Table follows SEC methodology: it reports the grant-date fair value of any new equity grants in the year. Because no new RSU grant was made to Jassy in 2025 (or since 2021), his 2025 table total is $2.07M — almost entirely security and travel costs. The economic value of RSUs vesting from the 2021 grant (FY2025: ~$43M vested) does not appear as a new grant in the 2025 table.
- The FY2025 total SBC expense charged to the income statement was $24.0B (FY2024: $22.0B; FY2023: $19.5B) — this is company-wide for ~1.6 million employees. The CEO's and CFO's individual RSU values are a negligible fraction of total SBC. [FY2025 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, p.36]
- Jeff Bezos (Executive Chair) received $81,840 in base salary with no equity grants reported in FY2025. His economic stake is through his ~8.8% ownership (~950M shares) which is not a compensation item. [Web: 2026 DEF 14A, web-sourced, unverified]

## 2. Performance Metrics

| Plan | Metric | Weight | Per-Share/Returns or Size-Based? | Source |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Annual bonus | **None** — no annual cash incentive plan for named executive officers except at new hire | N/A | N/A — no annual bonus plan exists | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B; Capital IQ Takeover Defenses: "no executive severance agreements; no annual cash incentives"; Web: 2026 DEF 14A (web-sourced, unverified) |
| Long-term incentive (RSU) — primary vehicle | **Time-vested only** — RSUs vest on a fixed schedule regardless of financial performance; the only implicit metric is stock price (shares vest into common equity; realized value = shares × stock price at vesting) | 100% | **Per-share (implicit, via stock price)** — no ROIC, no EPS, no operating income, no revenue, no TSR hurdle required; vesting is purely time-based | Capital IQ Takeover Defenses (compensation section): "compensation tied to long-term performance reflected primarily in the stock price"; FY2025 10-K, Note 1 (stock-based compensation accounting policy, p.44): "RSUs vest based on service period"; Web: 2026 DEF 14A philosophy statement; ggsitc.com executive compensation teardown (web-sourced, unverified) |
| Long-term incentive (RSU) — vesting schedule | Back-loaded time schedule: 5% year 1, 15% year 2, 40% year 3, 40% year 4 (CEO 2021 grant: 10-year schedule, >80% vesting in final 5 years of the grant, through 2031) | N/A | Per-share (time, no performance hurdle) | Web: Amazon RSU guides citing proxy disclosures (web-sourced, unverified); FY2025 10-K, p.1596–1599 (equity compensation policy) |

**Classification of each implicit metric:**

| Metric (implicit) | Explicit or Implicit? | Per-Share/Returns or Size-Based? | Incentive Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stock price appreciation | Implicit (no explicit target set) | Per-share | Executives benefit only if stock price rises; wealth tracks total shareholder return over a multi-year period |
| Operating income / ROIC | Not a metric | — | Not explicitly rewarded; no target or hurdle in the plan |
| Revenue / AWS growth | Not a metric | — | Not explicitly rewarded |
| EPS (diluted) | Not a metric | — | Not set as a threshold |
| Absolute EBITDA | Not a metric | — | Not set as a threshold |

**Conclusion on metrics:** Amazon uses exclusively time-vested RSUs with no explicit performance hurdles of any kind. No annual bonus plan. No LTIP with ROIC, EPS, or TSR hurdles. The link to per-share value is entirely through stock price — but it is implicit and unconditional: executives receive shares regardless of operating performance, as long as they remain employed. This is a structurally unusual model among S&P 500 mega-caps. Its effect is directional: Jassy cannot earn a cash bonus by growing revenue but hurting margins; his wealth accumulates only if the stock price rises. However, it also means mediocre but stable performance would still vest shares, since there is no performance condition.

---

## 4. Incentive Alignment Read

Amazon's compensation model is the simplest in the S&P 500 mega-cap peer group: no annual bonus plan, no explicit performance metrics of any kind, and a single vehicle — time-vested restricted stock units — that link executive wealth entirely to stock price appreciation over a multi-year horizon. The stated philosophy (per the 2026 DEF 14A) is that this "directly aligns executives' compensation with the returns we deliver to shareholders." That claim has economic substance: Jassy cannot enrich himself by growing revenue while destroying margins; his financial outcome is bound to the equity market's verdict on Amazon's long-term per-share value. The biggest limitation of this model is that vesting is unconditional — there is no performance hurdle (no ROIC minimum, no TSR threshold, no EPS floor) that would prevent RSU vesting even if operating results deteriorated. A management team that ran the company at mediocre-but-stable results could still vest their full grant. In practice, the model has worked during the Jassy era because operating income grew 6.5x (FY2022–FY2025) and the stock re-rated, but this is not a structural protection — it is a favorable outcome that happened to coincide with the time-vested schedule.

The single biggest incentive signal: **management is paid in equity that they cannot convert to cash except by holding for years (the back-loaded vesting schedule), which removes the short-termism of quarterly earnings management**. It does not, however, create an explicit incentive to deliver returns above the cost of capital (ROIC) or to improve per-share metrics beyond the stock price.

**Verdict: Mixed.** The structure is directionally per-share-oriented (equity only, no revenue or EBITDA bonuses), but lacks explicit returns-based or per-share performance hurdles. The absence of an annual bonus or any size-based metric is a structural positive; the absence of any performance condition on RSU vesting is a structural limitation.

# Ownership & Insider Behavior — AMZN

**Reporting standard:** US GAAP. **Currency:** USD. **Fiscal year end:** December 31. **As of:** 2026-07-04.
**Jurisdiction:** US SEC (10-K, DEF 14A, Form 4, Schedule 13D/13G). **Partial-data cap applied:** Shareholder friendliness max 60 — no complete beneficial ownership table from the 2026 DEF 14A proxy is in the data pool; no comprehensive Form 4 transaction log or Capital IQ insider-transaction export is in the pool. Named insiders and float are available from the Capital IQ Public Company Profile (Jul 1, 2026) and FY2025 10-K Item 9B; web-sourced ownership/transaction data is labeled as such throughout.

---

## 1. Ownership

| Holder | % Held | Share Class | Bought or Granted? | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Jeffrey P. Bezos (Founder & Executive Chair) | ~8.8% (~882–950M shares) | Common stock (1 vote/share) | **Bought** — Bezos's entire stake originates from founding Amazon in 1994 and long-term retention; he has not received new RSU grants in his Executive Chair role; stake is being reduced through orderly open-market sales and charitable gifts | Web: 2026 DEF 14A beneficial ownership table as reported by multiple outlets (web-sourced, unverified); FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 (10b5-1 plan Nov 14, 2025) |
| Andrew R. Jassy (President & CEO) | <0.1% | Common stock (1 vote/share) | **Granted** — Jassy's equity comes from a back-loaded 10-year RSU grant made at his CEO appointment in July 2021 (61,000 shares total, ~$212M grant-date fair value); no open-market purchases | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 (10b5-1 plan Nov 14, 2025); agent 03 incentives cross-module; web-sourced, unverified for share count |
| Other insiders (aggregate — named officers + directors ex-Bezos) | <0.2% (estimated) | Common stock (1 vote/share) | **Granted** — all other executive officers hold RSUs granted as compensation; no disclosed open-market purchases by any named officer other than Bezos; board directors hold equity from director grants | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74; Capital IQ Public Company Profile, Jul 1, 2026 |
| Vanguard Group (institutional) | ~6.8% | Common stock | N/A — passive index ownership | Web: 2026 proxy / 13F filings as reported (web-sourced, unverified); Capital IQ Public Company Profile (Vanguard Capital Management listed as investor, Jul 1, 2026) |
| BlackRock (institutional) | ~6.8% | Common stock | N/A — passive index ownership | Web: 2026 proxy / 13F filings as reported (web-sourced, unverified) |
| State Street Corporation (institutional) | ~3.6% | Common stock | N/A — passive index ownership | Web: 13F filings as reported (web-sourced, unverified); Capital IQ Public Company Profile (State Street Corporation listed as investor, Jul 1, 2026) |
| Float (public) | 90.9% | Common stock (1 vote/share) | N/A | Capital IQ Public Company Profile, Jul 1, 2026 (delayed quote last updated Jul 1, 2026 10:28 AM) |

**Total named insider ownership %:** Bezos ~8.8%; all other named insiders (Jassy + other officers + board) combined estimated <0.5%. Total insider ownership approximately **9–9.5%** (web-sourced, unverified; the proxy beneficial ownership table is not in the data pool).

**Single-class structure.** Amazon has one class of common stock with one vote per share. The Capital IQ Takeover Defenses report (Jul 1, 2026) confirms: "Dual Class Stock: No"; "Common Stock Voting Rights: 1." Bezos's influence derives from economic stake size, not from any structural super-voting mechanism. [Capital IQ Takeover Defenses, Jul 1, 2026]

**Shares outstanding.** 10,757.1M shares as of Jul 1, 2026 (Capital IQ Public Company Profile). 10,757.1M × $239.59 = $2,576B market cap. Shares outstanding increased from 10,383M (Dec 2023) to 10,597M (Dec 2024) to 10,734M (Dec 2025) to 10,757M (Q1 2026) — a net increase of ~374M shares (3.6%) over two years driven by RSU vesting net of Bezos sales. [Capital IQ Historical Capitalization tab, FY2024–Q1 2026; FY2025 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Stockholders' Equity, p.40]

## 2. Insider Transactions (last 12 months)

**Pool data (FY2025 10-K Item 9B — November 2025 disclosures):**

|---|---|---:|---|---|---|

| Andrew R. Jassy (President & CEO) | Sell (planned) | Up to 142,224 shares through Dec 31, 2026 | Plan adopted Nov 14, 2025 | Rule 10b5-1(c) plan — RSU diversification sales, small vs total shares outstanding | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 |
| David A. Zapolsky (SVP, Chief Global Affairs & Legal Officer) | Sell (planned) | Up to 64,059 shares through Nov 30, 2026 | Plan adopted Nov 3, 2025 | Rule 10b5-1(c) plan | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 |
| Douglas J. Herrington (CEO Worldwide Amazon Stores) | Sell (planned) | Up to 132,937 shares through Dec 31, 2026 | Plan adopted Nov 10, 2025 | Rule 10b5-1(c) plan | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 |
| Keith B. Alexander (Director, not standing for re-election) | Sell (planned) | Up to 1,800 shares through Nov 4, 2026 | Plan adopted Nov 11, 2025 | Rule 10b5-1(c) plan; immaterial amount | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 |
| Shelley L. Reynolds (VP, Worldwide Controller) | Sell (planned) | Up to 9,744 shares through Nov 29, 2026 | Plan adopted Nov 11, 2025 | Rule 10b5-1(c) plan | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 |
| Brian T. Olsavsky (CFO) | Plan terminated (no shares sold under prior plan) | Prior plan: up to 53,249 shares | Terminated Nov 19, 2025 | Plan originally adopted May 20, 2025; terminated before execution period closed; no shares sold | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 |
| All named insiders (Q1 2026) | No new plans adopted | None | Jan–Mar 2026 | Q1 2026 10-Q Item 5 (Trading Arrangements): "None" — no new plans in Q1 2026 | Q1 2026 10-Q, Item 5, p.48 |

**Web-sourced context (labeled unverified):** Bezos conducted a ~$5 billion concentrated selling spree in July 2025 (approximately 25 million shares at ~$221–$233/share), executed under a pre-set 10b5-1 plan. From late 2025 onward, his Form 4 filings shifted primarily to charitable gift transactions (code "G") rather than open-market sales. As of June/July 2026, Bezos holds approximately 882–950 million shares (~8.8% of outstanding). [Web: 13finsight.com citing Form 4 filings; web-sourced, unverified; note: these figures may not be filed with EDGAR in the pool but are consistent with the 10-K's 10b5-1 plan disclosure.]

**Net insider activity: Net selling.** All disclosed plans involve sales; no named insider has filed an open-market purchase in the pool period. Bezos's plan covers up to 15 million shares — roughly 1.6% of his current stake — which is a gradual diversification rather than a wholesale exit. All sales are under pre-set 10b5-1(c) plans that were adopted in November 2025; all sales are pre-scheduled. The CFO (Olsavsky) terminated his plan before shares were sold, which removes the most CFO-departure-signal-sensitive selling from the table.

**No open-market buys.** No named insider or director has made an open-market purchase of Amazon shares in the disclosed 12-month period. This is consistent with Amazon's compensation model (RSUs, no stock-option grants requiring purchase) and does not represent an unusual pattern for a large-cap S&P 500 company. Amazon's executive team accumulated their shares primarily through career service (Bezos) or grant vesting (Jassy and other officers), not open-market conviction purchases.

**Distinction — bought vs granted:**
- Bezos: **Bought** (founder equity, held since 1994; not a grant).
- All other named insiders: **Granted** (RSUs from compensation packages; no documented open-market purchases by any current officer other than Bezos).

## 3. Pledging & Encumbrance

| Insider | Shares Pledged | % of Their Holding | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Jeffrey P. Bezos | 0 (no pledge disclosed) | 0% | FY2025 10-K (no insider pledge disclosure; the 10-K's only pledge reference is corporate-level: cash/securities pledged as collateral for real estate and third-party seller obligations — Note 3, p.54 and footnote to Note 5 on cash/securities); Capital IQ Takeover Defenses: no insider pledging provision triggered |
| All other named insiders | 0 (none disclosed) | 0% | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B and Notes to Financial Statements; disqualifier scan |

**No pledging disclosed.** The FY2025 10-K contains no disclosure of any executive officer or director pledging Amazon shares as collateral for personal loans. The note (FY2025 10-K, Note 3, p.54) that references "pledged assets" relates to Amazon the company pledging cash and real estate as collateral for letters of credit and tenant improvement leases — not insider share pledging. US proxy statements typically contain an anti-pledging / anti-hedging policy in the Compensation section; the 2026 DEF 14A (absent from the pool) would contain the formal policy. However, no material insider pledging is disclosed or evidenced in any pool filing.

**Cross-reference to `business-model/01_disqualifier-scan`:** Disqualifier #2 (>50% promoter/insider shares pledged) — Not triggered. The disqualifier scan explicitly states: "No controlling promoter / founding-family pledge structure exists. The 10-K... discloses no material insider pledging." [business-model/01_disqualifier-scan.md, Disqualifier #2]

## 4. Control Structure

| Feature | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dual-class / super-voting | **None.** Amazon has a single class of common stock with one vote per share. "Dual Class Stock: No"; "Common Stock Voting Rights: 1"; "Time-Phased Unequal Voting Rights: No." | Capital IQ Takeover Defenses, Jul 1, 2026 |
| Controlled-company status | **No.** Amazon does not qualify as a "controlled company" under Nasdaq listing rules — no single holder owns >50% of voting power. Bezos holds ~8.8%; even combined with the other named insiders (<0.5%), total insider voting power is well below 50%. | Capital IQ Takeover Defenses, Jul 1, 2026; Capital IQ Public Company Profile (float 90.9%), Jul 1, 2026 |
| Shareholder bloc with board rights | **None.** No shareholder agreement, voting trust, or side agreement grants any holder board nomination or veto rights. Bezos's influence is through economic stake size only. The Nominating & Corporate Governance Committee nominates directors; shareholders elect them by majority vote (not plurality). | Capital IQ Takeover Defenses, Jul 1, 2026; 2026 DEF 14A (web-sourced, unverified) |
| Classified / staggered board | **None.** All 11 nominees stand for annual election. "Classified Board: No." | Capital IQ Takeover Defenses, Jul 1, 2026 |
| Poison pill | **None.** "Active Poison Pill: None Reported." | Capital IQ Takeover Defenses, Jul 1, 2026 |
| Bezos chair/CEO separation | CEO and Chair roles are separated: Jassy (CEO) and Bezos (Executive Chair). A Lead Independent Director (Jamie Gorelick) presides over executive sessions. | FY2025 10-K, p.4–5; 2026 DEF 14A (web-sourced, unverified) |
| Controlling-owner objective alignment (Filter 6) | **Not a Filter 6 concern.** Bezos is a founder who built Amazon over three decades, holds his equity primarily for long-term economic appreciation, and has no structural mechanism to extract value at the expense of minority shareholders (no dual class, no special dividend to himself, no related-party transactions). The company operates with no government ownership, is not a subsidiary of a parent, and is not a sprawling unrelated conglomerate (its segments — retail, cloud, advertising — are operationally integrated). Filter 6 (RF-OWN-004) does not apply. | CLAUDE.md §24 Filter 6; Module_Rules.md Score Cap Rules |

**Unaligned-owner test (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 6):**
(a) **Government control:** Not applicable — Amazon is a private corporation, no government ownership.
(b) **Listed subsidiary of a parent:** Not applicable — Amazon is the parent, not a subsidiary.
(c) **Sprawling unrelated-diversified conglomerate:** Not applicable — Amazon's three segments (North America retail, International retail, AWS) are operationally integrated around the same customer, technology, and logistics base; advertising serves retail; AWS serves enterprise. This is a multi-product platform, not an unrelated conglomerate.

No RF-OWN-004 flag applies. No shareholder-friendliness cap from Filter 6. The controlling-owner's objective (Bezos as the largest individual holder) is long-term per-share value appreciation; his incentives are aligned with minority holders, not opposed to them.

## 4A. Market Conduct

| Insider buys/sells vs subsequent results (timing) | Bezos conducted a ~$5 billion selling spree in July 2025 (~25M shares at $221–$233). Amazon stock subsequently rose to $278 by late 2025 before retreating. The selling occurred before Q2 2025 results (which beat consensus by $5.6B revenue and $0.36 EPS). The selling was executed under a pre-set 10b5-1 plan adopted before the quarter closed — this is the structural protection that pre-set plans provide against insider-timing allegations. Amazon beat consensus in all four quarters covering this period. The selling preceded strong results, not weak ones, which is the opposite of the adverse timing pattern. | FY2025 10-K, Item 9B, p.74 (10b5-1 plan disclosures); Web: Form 4 filings via 13finsight.com (web-sourced, unverified); Capital IQ Estimates Surprise tab (beat data) |

| Exchange clarification sought for a price move | None disclosed or evidenced. Amazon is a US NASDAQ-listed company; NASDAQ does not typically issue query letters for price moves at large-caps. No unusual regulatory exchange enquiry is evidenced in the pool. | FY2025 10-K; pool extracts |

## 5. Ownership / Insider Read

Bezos owns roughly 8.8% of Amazon, and that stake originates from founding the company — not from grants or option exercises. This is the most meaningful single fact: the largest individual shareholder built what he owns over three decades. All other named insiders (Jassy, Olsavsky, and the rest of the executive team) hold RSU grants with no evidence of open-market purchases, meaning their alignment is real but shallower and grant-dependent, not conviction-driven cash investment.

The net insider signal is selling, but it is entirely pre-scheduled under Rule 10b5-1(c) plans — the structural equivalent of saying "I will sell on a pre-set schedule regardless of what I know." Bezos's selling preceded strong quarterly results, not weak ones, and the CFO's plan was terminated before any sales. There is no adverse timing signal.

The biggest control point for minority holders is the absence of a dual-class structure. Bezos's ~8.8% stake gives him no special voting leverage beyond his economic size; the board is elected annually by majority vote; no poison pill or staggered board exists; and the Lead Independent Director is structurally independent of him. Amazon is one of the rare founder-chaired mega-caps where the founder's influence is purely proportional to his economic stake — a positive structural feature for minority holders.

**Note:** Amazon has no controlling promoter / family holding company structure. Item 13 (Certain Relationships and Related Transactions) is incorporated by reference to the 2026 proxy. The proxy (web-sourced) confirms no material related-party transaction other than the routine, immaterial ordinary-course payments to Weeks-affiliated (Corning) and Ng-affiliated (DeepLearning.AI) entities — both reviewed and cleared by the Board as not impairing independence. The core leakage question is answered: no value is leaking to a promoter or related group. The economic interests of the Board and management are aligned with public shareholders, not with a separate controlling entity.

**Overall takeover-defense assessment:** Amazon's charter and bylaw structure is notably shareholder-friendly for a large-cap US company. No poison pill. No staggered board. No dual-class shares. Majority (not plurality) director voting. No supermajority amendment requirements. Proxy access at market terms. Shareholders can call meetings at 25%. The only defensive features are blank-check preferred stock (a standard Delaware provision), a 90-day advance notice window (standard), and the Board's unilateral authority to resize its own board — all of which are conventional. The absence of dual-class stock is a key positive: Bezos' influence flows from his 8.8% economic stake, not from superior voting rights.

The opposition peaked at 43.9% in 2022 and has partially declined but remained persistently at 22% in both 2024 and 2025. 22% against is above the 20% materiality threshold. | Web: Morningstar (web-sourced, unverified); 2026 DEF 14A (web-sourced, unverified, citing 78% at "2025 Annual Meeting") |

| Dilution history | Shares outstanding grew from 10,383M (Dec 2023) to 10,731M (Dec 2025) — a net increase of 348M shares (+3.4%) over two years, entirely from RSU vesting; $6.1B of the $10B buyback authorization from March 2022 remains unused as of Dec 2025. The buyback program is dormant while the company reinvests heavily in AI capex. | FY2025 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Stockholders' Equity, p.40; Note 8, p.62 |

**Say-on-pay flag:** At 22% against in 2024 and 2025, Amazon's say-on-pay opposition exceeds the 20% red-flag threshold in the Red-Flag Trigger Engine. The trend has improved materially (from 44% in 2022) but has plateaued at 22%. This is an ongoing governance friction point, though it does not implicate fraud, self-dealing, or entrenchment. It reflects continued disagreement between institutional shareholders / proxy advisors and the Board on pay quantum and structure.

## 5. Minority-Shareholder Protection Read

Amazon's board is genuinely independent in structure: 83% independent directors, all major committees fully independent and chaired by independents, a Lead Independent Director (Gorelick) who engages directly with shareholders, majority voting for directors, and no defensive measures that suppress shareholder voice. The chair/CEO split (Bezos/Jassy) is real — Bezos' influence is economic (8.8% ownership), not structural (he has one vote per share, same as every other shareholder). There is no dual-class shield, no classified board, no supermajority protection, and no poison pill. Rights — special meetings at 25%, written consent at 50%, proxy access, no supermajority barrier — are better than typical for a company of this size and complexity.

The single biggest risk to minority holders is not structural but behavioral: the Board's compensation committee has failed to bring say-on-pay support above 80% despite three years of effort, and ISS has recommended against management's pay proposals in three consecutive years. This is a governance friction point that cannot be dismissed, even as it has materially improved from the 2022 nadir. The long tenures of Stonesifer (29 years) and Rubinstein (15 years) raise standard questions about director freshness, though no evidence of captured independence exists.

Additionally, Wendell Weeks — Audit Committee member — is a sitting CEO and Chair of Corning Incorporated; his dual commitment is a mild structural concern. Brad Smith's recent departure from Humana (April 2025) reduced one overboarding concern.

There is no §24 Filter 6 (Structurally Unaligned Controlling Owner) concern here. Bezos' ownership aligns his interests with per-share value; he does not control a separate parent entity extracting value from Amazon, nor is Amazon a subsidiary of a value-maximizing third party. The RF-OWN-004 filter does not trip.

**Verdict: Adequate.** The board is structurally independent, rights are intact and genuinely shareholder-friendly, and no entrenchment mechanism is in place. The persistent ~22% say-on-pay opposition and the long tenure of two directors keep the rating from "strong protection."

The score sits at the boundary between adequate and strong governance. The structural features (no dual-class, no pill, no staggered board, majority voting) are genuinely shareholder-friendly. No entrenchment mechanism is in place.

# Candor & Disclosure Quality — AMZN

**Reporting standard:** US GAAP. **Currency:** USD. **Fiscal year end:** December 31. **Filing regime:** US SEC. **As of:** 2026-07-04.

**Data available:** Five earnings transcripts (Q2 2025–Q1 2026), three annual shareholder letters (FY2023–FY2025), FY2025 10-K, FY2024 10-K, FY2023 10-K, Q1 2026 10-Q, Capital IQ Financials / Estimates exports. Cross-module inputs: `earnings/06_earnings-quality.md` (available), `earnings/04_guidance-consensus.md` (available), `management-governance/01_management-and-track-record.md` (available). **No proxy (DEF 14A) in pool** — compensation discussion not available; this affects the non-GAAP section only marginally (Amazon does not issue formal adjusted-EBIT tables) and does not cap this agent.

## 1. Owning the Misses

From `01_management-and-track-record`, the checkable promises over FY2023–FY2025 were: AWS re-acceleration, International profitability, cost-to-serve reduction, operating income recovery, and the FCF compression that accompanied the AI capex surge.

---

## 2. Non-GAAP / Adjustment Aggressiveness

Amazon does not publish a formal adjusted EBITDA or adjusted EBIT table. Its only official non-GAAP metric is Free Cash Flow (reconciled on FY2025 10-K p.28). Analysis uses `earnings/06_earnings-quality.md` as the primary cross-check.

| Signal | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Recurring "one-off" addbacks** | Amazon does not publish adjusted operating income tables, so there is no formal addback list. However, management verbally presents "ex-charges" operating income in transcripts when material charges occur — Q3 2025 ($4.3B charges) and Q4 2025 ($2.4B charges). This verbal adjustment is reasonable and disclosed. The concern is that restructuring/severance has appeared in every recent year at a baseline of ~$700M–$800M (FY2023, FY2024) and spiked in FY2025 ($4.6B with non-recurring components). Management treats each year's charge as a one-off; the cumulative pattern is not acknowledged. | Q3 2025 transcript, Oct 30, 2025, pp.7–8; Q4 2025 transcript, Feb 5, 2026, p.9; earnings/06_earnings-quality.md §5 (five-year restructuring pattern) |
| **GAAP-to-adjusted gap (magnitude / trend)** | The most important gap is at the reported EPS level: FY2025 reported diluted EPS of $7.17 vs Capital IQ Normalized EPS of $4.70 — a 34.5% inflation from the $15.3B pre-tax investment gain (Anthropic reclassification + Rivian). This recurs: FY2021 +$14.7B gain, FY2022 −$15.9B loss, FY2025 +$15.3B gain. At the operating income line (the number management focuses on), the GAAP-to-adjusted gap is minor: FY2025 GAAP operating income was $80.0B; management's verbal "ex-charges" figure for Q3 and Q4 combined amounts to ~$86.7B ($80.0B + $4.3B Q3 + $2.4B Q4), a ~8% uplift. | earnings/06_earnings-quality.md §7; FY2025 10-K, Item 7, p.27; Capital IQ Income Statement |
| **Does adjusted framing flatter reality?** | For operating income: the verbal adjustments are defensible — they strip out genuine one-time legal settlements ($2.5B FTC, $1.1B Italy tax) and asset impairments. Calling all severance non-recurring is aggressive but not fraudulent. For EPS: Amazon does not formally issue adjusted EPS guidance. The $7.17 reported EPS overstates operating earnings quality by 34%; this is a genuine concern, but Amazon's management consistently directs attention to operating income and CFO rather than net income or reported EPS, which partially mitigates the risk that the misleading reported EPS number is being actively promoted. The two consecutive server useful-life changes (5→6yr Jan 2024, 6→5yr Jan 2025) are disclosed fully on 10-K Note 1, p.41–42 and p.47, though the back-and-forth is unusual for a $301B+ asset base. | earnings/06_earnings-quality.md §7, §8 (Accounting Trap Checklist: change in useful life, score 35/100 severity); FY2025 10-K, Note 1, p.41–42 |
| **SBC exclusion from "adjusted" figures** | SBC of $19.5B in FY2025 (2.7% of revenue; 24.3% of EBIT) is excluded from Capital IQ Normalized EPS. Amazon does not formally promote adjusted EPS excluding SBC, but analyst models universally strip it. At $1.80/share, it is a real economic cost worth flagging. Amazon does not attempt to hide SBC: it is prominently disclosed in Note 4 (p.53 of FY2025 10-K) and is a separate CFO reconciliation item. | earnings/06_earnings-quality.md §8; FY2025 10-K, Note 4, p.53 |

**Non-GAAP verdict: Conservative at the operating income level; noisy at the reported EPS level due to inherent equity investment accounting.** Management does not run an aggressive addback program. The single largest distortion (Anthropic mark-to-market) is structural to the business and fully disclosed, though the size of the swing ($15.3B in FY2025, −$15.9B in FY2022) is large enough to materially mislead anyone relying on headline EPS.

---

## 3. Disclosure Transparency

Amazon discloses three reportable segments (North America, International, AWS) with revenue, operating income, and depreciation broken out per Note 10 of the 10-K (p.67–68 of the FY2025 10-K). Within AWS, management provides an annualized revenue run rate and backlog ($364B at Q1 2026 close, stated on Q1 2026 earnings call and confirmed in the 10-Q) but does not break out AI vs core AWS revenue — a notable gap given the scale of AI claims. The company separately discloses advertising services revenue ($56.0B in FY2025), which has become one of its highest-margin businesses, as a separate revenue line but not as a segment with disclosed operating income. Free cash flow is reconciled in the 10-K. KPI disclosure has been consistent period-over-period: the same segment structure, the same revenue breakdowns, and the same FCF reconciliation appear in each annual filing. There is no reduction in transparency over the period reviewed. The one watch point is the deliberate non-disclosure of capex split between maintenance and growth — management acknowledges this limitation in every transcript but does not rectify it, which is a recurring analyst frustration. Overall segment economics are accessible and consistent; the main gap is the absence of an AI-specific revenue or margin disclosure within AWS, which would be the single most useful new disclosure given the $200B capex bet.

---

## 4. Tone in Bad Times

Q3 2025 was the worst recent quarter by operating income miss: $17.4B reported vs guidance of $19.0B–$22.0B high end, driven by a $4.3B combined special charge. The tone was candid. Jassy led his prepared remarks by stating the reported number, then immediately explaining the two charges with dollar amounts — not leading with the "adjusted" figure or the AWS acceleration. The Q&A on the Q3 2025 call addressed the FTC settlement directly (one question from Justin Post implicitly sought confidence in capacity and demand, which Jassy answered substantively). No question on the FTC settlement itself appeared in the Q&A transcript, which likely reflects that management had quantified it so clearly in the prepared remarks that analysts had no follow-up ambiguity. Q4 2025 adopted the same pattern: three charges named and quantified in Olsavsky's second paragraph, before any business update. On the Q4 2025 call, analysts pressed on FCF guardrails and ROIC, and Jassy gave a direct answer — referencing the prior AWS build cycle, acknowledging uncertainty, and declining to set a specific FCF floor — rather than deflecting. The tone in both calls was promotional in presenting the business opportunity (AI, grocery, Leo) but candid in presenting the financial results, including the charges.

---

## 5. Candor Read

Management's communications in bad periods hold up. When results were below guidance (Q3 2025, Q4 2025), the charges were named, sized, and attributed to their cause in the first substantive paragraph of prepared remarks — not buried in footnotes or discovered by analysts in the Q&A. The FCF compression was pre-disclosed and then confirmed without spin. The single biggest candor signal, positive in nature, is the combination of pre-warning on FCF compression (FY2024 letter, Apr 2025) and then delivering exactly the warned outcome without retroactive framing. The one legitimate concern is the treatment of restructuring costs: $700M–$800M annually in "other operating expense" in FY2023–FY2024 that gets called non-recurring each year, and the FY2025 spike to $4.6B that blends genuine one-offs (FTC, Italy) with what has become a recurring baseline of severance and reorganization. The two-direction server useful-life change (5→6yr in 2024, back to 6→5yr in 2025) is disclosed clearly but has never been explained in a way that acknowledges the earnings-management optics. The no-integrity-flag-routed status from `business-model/01_disqualifier-scan` means there is no unresolved adverse signal compounding this read. **Verdict: candid / high-trust.** The evidence for this verdict is specific: charges disclosed immediately and accurately, FCF compression pre-signaled, operating income (not reported EPS) foregrounded, and no history of guidance set-to-miss being obscured. The one area short of ideal is the recurring-restructuring pattern.

# Valuation Module — AMZN (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Amazon (AMZN) is modestly overvalued at $238.34, trading 13.5% above the base-case fair value of $210 per share. The bull / base / bear fair-value levels are $247 / $210 / $146, driven primarily by the sum-of-the-parts analysis (40% weight), which anchors on audited FY2025 segment EBIT and finds the current price sits 40% above the trailing breakup value of the business. The reverse-DCF shows the market is pricing in 16.4% annual profit growth for a full decade — plausible for three to five years given AWS growing at 28%, but aggressive as a ten-year requirement. The margin of safety is negative at −13.5%, while the downside to the bear case is 38.7% — a loss from $238 to $146 — driven by a simultaneous AWS deceleration, D&A step-up, and multiple compression. At today's price, no cushion exists against a base-case miss; the stock is a bet on excellent, not merely good, execution.

---

## 1. Valuation Verdict

- **Verdict:** Modestly overvalued
- **Base-case fair value (point, per share):** $210
- **Current price:** $238.34 (July 1, 2026 last close, pool-verified; Capital IQ Key Stats, three-way cross-confirmed)
- **Bull / Base / Bear fair-value levels (points):** $247 / $210 / $146
- **Cross-method dispersion (football field, low–high):**
  - Gordon DCF (04, floor): $104/share
  - SOTP bear (06): $129/share
  - SOTP base (06): $170/share
  - DCF exit 10x (04): $207/share
  - SOTP bull (06): $221/share
  - Peers (03, NTM EV/EBITDA 13x warranted): $258/share
  - Peers / NTM EV/Sales (03, high end): $284/share
  - *Full football field (value-producing methods):* $104 – $284/share
  - *Excluding Gordon DCF floor (primary working range):* $129 – $284/share
- **Valuation attractiveness /100** *(higher = cheaper)*: **38**
- **Margin of safety /100** *(higher = better)*: **0** (negative; price exceeds base fair value; no cushion exists)
- **Valuation confidence /100:** **55** (capped at 60 due to terminal value > 75% of DCF EV; further capped at 55 due to cross-method spread > 40% unreconciled on the full range including the Gordon floor)
- **Downside risk /100** *(higher = worse — inverted score)*: **72** (38.7% downside to the bear case of $146)
- **Data quality /100:** **88** (all five methods ran; pool-verified price; 53–57 broker consensus; full segment data through FY2025; three audited annual reports; 10-Q through Q1 2026; fresh peer comp set as of July 1, 2026; zero extraction failures)
- **Overall usefulness /100:** **78**
- **Dominant valuation method (one line):** SOTP at $170 (40% weight) — the most transparent and reproducible method, anchored on audited FY2025 segment EBIT; AWS alone accounts for 66% of the gross enterprise value in the base case, making the SOTP the clearest lens for a multi-segment conglomerate where cloud and retail warrant structurally different multiples.
- **What's priced in (one line):** At $238.34, the market prices 16.4% annual NOPAT growth for ten years — implying $3.27T in revenue and $304B in NOPAT by FY2035, versus the base-case DCF forecast of $2.01T revenue and $207B NOPAT; aggressive as a decade-long requirement, plausible for three to five years given AWS at 28% growth. [05_reverse-dcf.md §2, §5]
- **Biggest valuation risk (one line):** The D&A step-up from the $170B+ annualized AI capex wave — the single highest-impact EBIT variable — runs 6–24 months ahead of customer billings; if the billing lag extends to the long end, EBIT is simultaneously compressed and the multiple contracts, producing a 38.7% downside to $146. [07_earnings-sensitivity.md §3 via 07_scenario-and-fair-value.md §3]

---

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation *(CLAUDE.md §8)*

- **Strongest bear point:** The SOTP on audited FY2025 EBIT ($170 base, $129 bear) finds the current price is 40%–85% above trailing breakup value, meaning almost the entire current market cap rests on future earnings the business has not yet delivered. If AWS growth decelerates from 28% to 20% while the D&A step-up runs at the worst-case 24-month billing lag, consolidated EBIT in FY2026–FY2027 could fall well below consensus ($103.8B FY2026 consensus EBIT), and the multiple would compress simultaneously. [06_sum-of-the-parts.md §4; 07_scenario-and-fair-value.md §3]

- **Strongest bull point:** On a pure forward-multiple basis, the peer-warranted NTM EV/EBITDA of 13.0x (a 14% premium to the heterogeneous peer median for a business with AWS at $364B backlog growing at 28%) implies $258/share — 8% above today. The current price of 11.9x NTM EV/EBITDA is actually *below* the warranted multiple for a company with AWS quality and growth. If D&A absorption follows the short-lag scenario (6–12 months), FCF recovers faster than consensus and the multiple holds or expands to the bull 14x. [03_relative-valuation-peers.md §5–6; 07_scenario-and-fair-value.md §3]

- **Single killer risk:** Terminal-value dominance (79.9% of DCF EV from the Gordon terminal) means the intrinsic value rests almost entirely on assumptions about Amazon's competitive position and growth rate in 2035 — a decade out. Any material change to the terminal multiple (from 10x to 8x EV/EBITDA at FY2035) shaves $38/share from the DCF anchor; if the moat erodes (09_moat.md currently finds a narrow moat with ROIC of 9.0% below WACC of 10.4–11.2%), the entire valuation framework shifts down. [04_intrinsic-dcf.md §5; 09_moat.md §5]

- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** Through-cycle ROIC (9.0%) is below WACC (10.4–11.2%), meaning Amazon has not yet proven it earns above its cost of capital on a through-cycle basis — a business at or below its cost of capital does not warrant an open-ended premium. The strict FCF turned negative in LTM (CFO $148.5B minus capex $151.0B = −$2.5B), confirming the investment cycle is consuming all free cash flow and then some. [09_moat.md §3; 01_price-and-capital-structure.md §3]

---

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| Specialist | Verdict Line | Biggest Finding |

| multiples-own-history | AMZN sits at the 13th–26th percentile of its own 18-month multiple band on forward metrics (EV/NTM EBITDA 11.93x vs 18-month median 12.96x; −8%) | Own-history window of only 18 months is too short for reliable reversion — Amazon's structural earnings inflection (EBIT margin from 2.6% FY2022 to 13.1% Q1 2026) means pre-2024 multiples are not a valid comparator; flagged as "illustrative only, not a fair-value input" |
| relative-valuation-peers | Base-case peer fair value: $258/share (NTM EV/EBITDA at warranted 13.0x); current price is 8.1% below warranted — slight discount on the peer method alone | AMZN trades at just 4.6% NTM EV/EBITDA premium to a peer median pulled down by low-margin physical retailers; the peer discount vs. megacap-tech-quality peers is misleading — the warranted premium is ~13x vs current 11.93x |
| intrinsic-dcf | Gordon base: $104/share (128% premium of price to Gordon intrinsic); exit-multiple anchor: $207/share (10x FY2035 EBITDA at WACC 10.4%) | Gordon DCF is terminal-dominated (TV = 79.9%) and produces a structurally depressed number due to three years of deeply negative FCF (FY2026–FY2028) compounded at 10.4%; exit-multiple is the more informative lens: current price implies 10–12x FY2035 EBITDA, requiring execution across a full decade |
| reverse-dcf | Market prices in 16.4% NOPAT CAGR for 10 years (FY2026–FY2035), implying NOPAT of $304B and revenue of $3.27T by FY2035 | Aggressive for the full decade; plausible for 3–5 years given AWS at 28% growth; D&A step-up timing is the dominant swing input — a 41.75% implied growth rate would result from using the company-disclosed FCF ($11.2B) instead of normalized NOPAT ($66.6B), confirming the FCF base is the most sensitive input |
| sum-of-the-parts | SOTP base: $170/share (FY2025 audited EBIT: 28x/20x/15x); LTM base ~$182; bull $221; bear $129; current price is 40% above the FY2025 base SOTP | AWS generates 66% of gross EV at the base case ($1.277T of $1.941T) on 57% of EBIT but only 18% of revenue; the current $238 price is almost entirely a bet on AWS multiple expansion or AWS EBIT growth beyond what FY2025 reflects; North America and International together contribute only $664B to gross EV |
| scenario-and-fair-value | Bull/Base/Bear: $247/$210/$146; margin of safety −13.5%; downside to bear 38.7% | Blended base fair value $210 (35% peers × $258 + 25% DCF exit × $207 + 40% SOTP × $170); method dispersion 148% (Gordon to peers), narrowing to 52% once Gordon is replaced by exit multiple; D&A step-up timing is the dominant swing factor between scenarios |

---

## 3. Reconciliation

**Methods disagree materially — the full method dispersion of 148% (Gordon DCF $104 to peers $258) exceeds the 40% flag threshold.**

The three primary working methods (peers at $258, DCF exit at $207, SOTP at $170) still span 52% from SOTP to peers, which also exceeds the 40% flag. This disagreement is genuine but structurally explained:

**SOTP ($170, base) vs. Peers ($258):** The $88/share gap reflects a timing difference, not a disagreement about Amazon's value as a business. SOTP anchors on audited FY2025 trailing EBIT ($79.975B) and applies segment multiples — producing the trailing breakup value. Peers anchor on FY2026 consensus NTM EBITDA ($222.6B, +43% above FY2025 GAAP EBITDA) and assign a quality-adjusted multiple to that forward earnings power. The 43% EBITDA growth priced into consensus is the bridge between $170 and $258 — the SOTP will approach the peer implied value if and when FY2026 EBITDA is delivered. SOTP is trusted most as the conservative floor; peers as the forward upper bound.

**DCF exit ($207) bridges the gap** — by using the exit-multiple framework applied to the 10-year terminal EBITDA ($563B), it incorporates both the current capex cycle drag and the eventual franchise value. The Gordon DCF ($104) is treated as a methodological floor, not a fair value, because the deep negative FCFs in FY2026–FY2028 are an artifact of the timing mismatch between capex recognition and revenue billing, not a permanent impairment. The Gordon method is retained in the football field for transparency but excluded from the weighted blend at `07`'s direction.

**Reconciled view:** Trust the SOTP most for the floor (audited, segment-level data, transparent multiples), peers for the forward ceiling, and DCF exit as the franchise value bridge. Base fair value $210 is the honest weighted blend of these three methods. The divergence above $210 and below $258 is real and should not be averaged away — it represents the uncertainty in whether FY2026 earnings delivery materializes as consensus projects.

| Terminal value >75% of DCF EV | **Y** | Valuation confidence | Cap at 60; Gordon DCF TV = 79.9% of EV (04_intrinsic-dcf.md §5); this cap is dominated by the methods-disagree cap of 55 |

**Multiple caps on the same score:** Methods-disagree cap (55) is more restrictive than the terminal-dominance cap (60) — final confidence cap is **55**.

---

## 5. Fair-Value Summary

The bull / base / bear fair-value levels are $247 / $210 / $146, with the SOTP at $170 (40% weight) driving the base case below the current price. AWS generates 66% of the gross enterprise value in the base SOTP despite contributing only 18% of revenue — the stock is effectively a leveraged bet on the AWS cloud franchise. The peer-forward method at $258 (35% weight) anchors on FY2026 consensus NTM EBITDA ($222.6B) and shows that the current 11.9x NTM EV/EBITDA is modestly below the warranted 13.0x — meaning on a purely forward-multiple basis the stock is not overpriced. The tension is between the trailing-EBIT breakup value ($170) and the forward-earnings power ($258); the $210 base is the honest compromise weighted toward the trailing anchor.

At $238.34, the current price implies 10.7x NTM EV/EBITDA on the blended basis — below the warranted 13x on the peer method but above what the trailing SOTP supports. The reverse-DCF shows the market is pricing 16.4% NOPAT CAGR for a decade, requiring $3.27T in revenue by FY2035; that is aggressive for a 10-year window but plausible for 3–5 years given AWS growing at 28% and a $364B backlog.

The margin of safety is negative at −13.5%: the stock trades 13.5% above the $210 base case, meaning there is no cushion if the base case is right. The downside to the bear case is 38.7%: a fall from $238 to $146 requires simultaneous AWS deceleration (28% → 20%), D&A step-up at the worst-case billing lag, advertising softening to 12% growth, and a multiple compression to 10.5x NTM EV/EBITDA. These three risks are correlated — they all move together in an adverse macro or execution scenario — making the bear case more likely than its individual probabilities suggest.

This is not value-trap risk in the classical sense: Amazon has no misaligned owner, no government controller, no holdco structure, and no structural impediment to earnings realization. The risk is execution risk — specifically, whether the AI capex wave ($170B+ annualized) monetizes within 6–12 months (the bull) or 18–24 months (the bear). At the current price, the market has priced in near-perfect execution with no room for the base case, let alone the bear.

---

## 6. What Would Change The Valuation Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Make It Cheaper | What Would Make It More Expensive | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Modestly overvalued | Stock falls to $185–$200 without a change in fundamentals (bringing it to parity with or below the $210 base); OR FY2026 EBITDA comes in materially above the $211B consensus, closing the gap between the trailing SOTP and the forward multiple | Stock continues rising while fundamentals deteriorate — widening the gap above $247 without incremental evidence of AWS acceleration or margin expansion delivering ahead of schedule | Q2 2026 results (segment EBIT update — especially AWS growth trajectory and D&A rate); management Q2 guidance on capex cadence and billing-lag commentary |
| — | AWS decelerates below 25% growth (the 28% Q1 2026 trajectory reverses); D&A as a percent of AWS revenue rises faster than consensus (the billing-lag worst case materializes) | AWS accelerates beyond 30% growth; D&A as a share of revenue stabilizes or falls (billing lag shorter than 12 months); advertising re-rates toward software-like multiples on standalone potential | FY2026 Q2–Q3 AWS revenue growth and T&I cost-per-unit trajectory; any announcement about AWS pricing or capacity commitments |
| — | A material earnings miss vs. consensus (FY2026 EBIT below $95B) combined with a macro-driven multiple compression (broad market de-rate from AI capex concerns) | A strategic announcement — AWS spin-out or tracking stock; healthcare / physical retail restructuring that makes segments visible and separately valued — that unlocks the SOTP discount to the sum of parts | AWS standalone profitability disclosures at segment level (currently disclosed only within the three reportable segments); any capex guidance revision |

---

## 7. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Fair-value levels:** Bull $247 / Base $210 / Bear $146 per share. The base case rests on a 35/25/40 blend of peers (NTM EV/EBITDA, warranted 13x, $258), DCF exit-multiple (10x FY2035 EBITDA, $207), and SOTP (FY2025 audited EBIT at 28x/20x/15x, $170). No single method is clean; the SOTP at $170 is the most grounded anchor on today's earnings, and the peers at $258 reflect where the stock should trade if FY2026 consensus is delivered.

- **What's priced in:** The market is pricing 16.4% NOPAT CAGR for ten years, implying $3.27T in revenue by FY2035 — plausible for 3–5 years (AWS at 28% growth, $364B backlog), aggressive for a full decade. The current 11.9x NTM EV/EBITDA is modestly below the peer-warranted 13.0x — meaning if the base case is delivered, the stock is actually cheap on a forward multiple basis. The risk is not that the multiple is wrong, but that the earnings trajectory doesn't arrive.

- **Margin of safety vs. downside-to-bear:** Margin of safety = −13.5% (the stock is 13.5% above the $210 base fair value; no cushion). Downside to the bear = 38.7% (a fall from $238 to $146 if AWS decelerates, D&A step-up hits at the worst-case lag, and the multiple compresses). These are two separate reads: one tells you there is no cushion at today's price; the other tells you how much you can lose in the bad scenario. Both need to reach the master synthesizer separately.

- **Execution risk, not value-trap risk:** Amazon is not a value trap on ownership grounds. No government controller, no parent-subsidiary conflict, no unrelated conglomerate structure. RF-OWN-004 does not apply. The risk is that the current price prices in successful execution of the largest single capital-expenditure program in Amazon's history ($170B+ annualized for AI infrastructure). The warranted multiple exists if AWS grows as projected; the bear-case multiple (10.5x) is below the peer median precisely because execution misses carry a double-hit: lower earnings AND lower multiple simultaneously.

- **Which method to trust:** SOTP first (audited FY2025 segment EBIT, transparent multiples, grounded in reported numbers). Peer NTM EV/EBITDA second (forward earnings power, but peer set is heterogeneous — warranted-multiple adjustment of +1.59x above raw median is required). DCF exit multiple third (franchise value, but heavily dependent on 10-year revenue path). Gordon DCF last — treat as a floor ($104), not a fair value; the negative FCF in FY2026–FY2028 compounding at 10.4% mechanically destroys PV in a way that doesn't reflect the business's franchise value.

- **No partial-data cap applied** — all five methods ran, price is pool-verified, consensus is full (53–57 brokers). The confidence cap at 55 is driven by the >40% method dispersion and the terminal-value dominance of the DCF — both structural features of this company at this point in the investment cycle, not data gaps.

- **Highest-value next data request:** Q2 2026 earnings results (expected July/August 2026) — specifically (a) AWS revenue growth trajectory (will it sustain above 28% or begin decelerating?), (b) technology and infrastructure cost as a percent of revenue (the D&A step-up magnitude and billing-lag timing), and (c) management's FY2026 capex guidance update. These three data points would allow the scenario-and-fair-value model to narrow the $101/share bull-to-bear spread meaningfully.

- **Explicit handoff:** The master synthesizer's "Valuation and Peer Mispricing" section should defer to this synthesis for all fair-value inputs. The bull / base / bear fair-value levels ($247 / $210 / $146), the margin of safety (−13.5%), and the downside-to-bear (38.7%) are the inputs for the master's probability-weighted scenario model. The master synthesizer assigns the scenario probabilities and computes the probability-weighted return — that work does not belong here. This module's conclusion: the stock is modestly overvalued at $238.34, with no cushion against the base case and significant downside (38.7%) to the bear.

---

## 8. Simple Summary

- Amazon trades at $238.34, which is 13.5% above the base-case fair value of $210; the verdict is **modestly overvalued**
- Bull / Base / Bear fair-value levels: **$247 / $210 / $146**; bull-to-bear spread of $101/share
- The market is pricing 16.4% NOPAT growth per year for ten years — plausible for 3–5 years given AWS at 28% growth, aggressive as a full-decade requirement
- Downside to the bear is 38.7% (a fall from $238 to $146); upside to the bull is only +3.6% ($247); the asymmetry is notable — but the master synthesizer owns the probability weighting
- The method that matters most: **SOTP** ($170/share, 40% weight), anchored on audited FY2025 segment EBIT; AWS alone generates 66% of the gross enterprise value at base-case multiples, making this fundamentally an AWS valuation story
- No value-trap risk from ownership: no government controller, no misaligned parent, RF-OWN-004 not triggered; the risk is execution risk on the AI capex buildout
- Current price ($238.34) is pool-verified (July 1, 2026 last close, Capital IQ, three-way cross-confirmed); all price-relative scores are unlocked
- This module is useful to the master synthesizer (Overall usefulness 78/100); the key limit is the >40% method dispersion that caps confidence at 55, which is a feature of the AI investment cycle rather than a data gap

| **= Enterprise value (EV)** | **$2,656,300M ($2.656 trillion)** | $2,563,849 + $235,540 + 0 + 0 − $143,089 = **$2,656,300M**. Cross-check: Capital IQ Key Stats "Total Enterprise Value (TEV)" = $2,656,300.46M — zero discrepancy. |

**EV bridge arithmetic verification:** $2,563,849 + $235,540 − $143,089 = $2,656,300M ✓

**Cash quality note (§15 compliance).** The $143,089M netted as cash is operating cash and genuine short-term equivalents, net of restricted amounts. The Capital IQ figure has already excluded restricted/pledged cash (confirmed by the FY2025 10-K Note 2 reconciliation above). What is NOT netted: (a) $51,423M in long-term investments (Anthropic preferred stock ~$19–20B, Rivian equity ~$5B, other private-company equity/warrants) — these are strategic, carry mark-to-market volatility recorded in Other income/expense, and are not cash equivalents; (b) $41,273M in short-term investments — these ARE included in the netted figure per CIQ's standard treatment (money market funds, US government and agency securities, corporate debt at Level 1/2 — all liquid, short-duration, and equivalent to cash). The $41,273M in ST investments passes the cash-quality test: they are classified as Level 1 or Level 2 securities with maturities consistent with cash equivalents and do not include equity or long-tenor fair-value instruments (FY2025 10-K, Note 2, cash and investments table).

**Net debt / cash basis labeling (§15 strict / broad).** Two bases are carried forward:
- **Strict basis** (financial debt only, no lease liabilities): financial bonds + revolving credit + other borrowings = $130,598M (BS: $152M revolving + $3,172M current LTD + $127,274M LT debt); strict net cash = $143,089M − $130,598M = **$12,491M net cash**. [Balance Sheet, Form 10-Q Q1 2026 (Apr-30-2026)]
- **Broad basis** (CIQ definition — total debt including lease liabilities): $235,540M total debt; broad net debt = $235,540M − $143,089M = **$92,451M net debt**. [Capital IQ Capital Structure Summary, Mar-31-2026]

The broad basis is the CIQ-computed figure ($92,451M) and is the canonical net-debt figure for leverage ratios, consistent with the earnings module. The strict basis ($12,491M net cash) is provided for financial-covenant and credit analysis where leases are excluded.

**Adjustments NOT made and why:**
- Operating lease liabilities: already included in Total Debt ($104,942M in CIQ's Total Debt). This is the canonical treatment for Amazon given the economic substance of its lease obligations (the 10-K states 3.8% weighted-average discount rate on operating leases with ~10-year average remaining term).
- Pensions / OPEB: Amazon has no US defined-benefit pension; immaterial foreign obligations exist but are not disclosed as material liabilities.
- Contingent claims: various legal proceedings but no accrued liability material enough to adjust EV (FY2025 10-K, Note 7 — Commitments and Contingencies).
- Long-term equity investments: not netted per operating-company standard (see cash quality note above).

**Leverage note.** On the broad basis (including $104.9B in lease liabilities), net debt is $92.5B, giving a 0.59× EBITDA ratio — very low leverage for a company of this scale. On the strict basis (financial bonds only), Amazon is in a net cash position of $12.5B. The large Q1 2026 increase in financial debt (bonds rose from $68B at FY2025 to $121.8B at Q1 2026, a $53.8B increase) reflects new senior note issuances to pre-fund the $151B annualized capex run-rate for AWS AI infrastructure. Even at the elevated Q1 2026 debt level, leverage is modest given $155.9B in LTM EBITDA.

**Partial-data context.** Capital IQ's quarterly Multiples tab export covers seven quarterly datapoints from December 2024 through June 2026 — approximately 18 months. The 18-month CIQ series is the only internally consistent multiple band available.

**Structural context that justifies the short window.** Amazon's EBIT margin expanded from 2.6% in FY2022 to 13.1% in Q1 2026. The business that traded at 30–40x EBIT or 15–20x EBITDA in the low-margin 2020–2023 era was structurally different — margins, FCF conversion, and AWS mix are now at levels not seen before in Amazon's history. The pre-2024 multiple history would conflate different earnings power levels with today's. The 18-month post-2024 band is therefore the most relevant comparable period available. ## 3. Re-Rating / De-Rating Read

Over the 18-month window (Dec 2024 to Jun/Jul 2026), the stock has **de-rated on forward multiples** and sits in the lower quartile of its own short-range band on EV/NTM EBITDA, EV/NTM EBIT, P/NTM EPS, and P/BV. The de-rating has been most pronounced on price-to-earnings metrics.

**EV/NTM EBITDA** — current 11.93x versus an 18-month mean of 12.96x and median of 12.98x: a discount of approximately **8% to both mean and median** (`(11.93 − 12.96) / 12.96 = −7.9%`; `(11.93 − 12.98) / 12.98 = −8.1%`). The 25th percentile of the range.

**P/NTM EPS** — current 28.49x versus mean of 31.50x and median of 31.01x: a discount of approximately **10% to the mean and 8% to the median** (`(28.49 − 31.50) / 31.50 = −9.6%`; `(28.49 − 31.01) / 31.01 = −8.1%`). The 15th percentile of the range.

**EV/LTM EBITDA** — current 15.4x versus mean of 16.17x and median of 16.13x: a discount of approximately **5% to both** (`(15.38 − 16.17) / 16.17 = −4.9%`). The 26th percentile.

The de-rating is driven by two forces. First, the LTM and NTM earnings metric in the denominator has grown rapidly — EPS up 51% LTM versus FY2024, EBITDA up 28% — which mechanically compresses the multiple even if the stock price holds. Second, the market has also partially stepped back from the peak Dec-2024 multiple (18.95x LTM EBITDA, 46.91x reported P/E at Dec-2024 close) — the stock traded at $229 in late 2024, rose to $265 by Mar-26-2026 (when it commanded 18.9x LTM EBITDA), then pulled back to $238. The net result is a ~5–10% compression versus the 18-month band average, reflecting a combination of rapid earnings growth and a modest multiple step-down. [Capital IQ Multiples tab quarterly close series; earnings/01_historical-financials.md LTM EPS and EBITDA figures]

## 4. Implied Value from Reversion

**Illustrative-only. Per the partial-data rule: own history < 3 years. These numbers are directional and are NOT a fair-value input for `07_scenario-and-fair-value`.**

Formula used throughout: `Implied EV = multiple × metric; Implied equity = Implied EV − total debt (broad, $235,540M) + cash ($143,089M); Implied per-share = Implied equity / 10,874M diluted shares`. For P/E: implied per-share = multiple × NTM EPS directly (no EV bridge).

| Multiple | Reversion target (median) | Reversion target (mean) | Metric used | Implied price (median) | Implied price (mean) | vs Current $238.34 (median) |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| EV / NTM EBITDA | 12.98x | 12.96x | FY2026 consensus EBITDA $211,027M | $243 | $243 | +2.1% |
| EV / LTM EBITDA | 16.13x | 16.17x | LTM EBITDA (CIQ adj.) ~$172,700M | $265 | $266 | +11.2% |
| EV / NTM EBIT | 26.76x | 26.92x | FY2026 consensus EBIT $103,833M | $247 | $249 | +3.6% |
| P / NTM EPS | 31.01x | 31.50x | NTM EPS (CIQ rolling) $8.37 | $259 | $264 | +8.7% |

**Calculations (median, for verification):**
- EV/NTM EBITDA: `12.98 × 211,027 = $2,739,130M EV; equity = 2,739,130 − 235,540 + 143,089 = $2,646,679M; per share = $2,646,679M / 10,874M = $243.40`
- EV/LTM EBITDA: `16.13 × 172,700 = $2,786,451M EV; equity = 2,786,451 − 235,540 + 143,089 = $2,694,000M; per share ≈ $247.75` (using CIQ-adjusted EBITDA) — alternatively at 16.13x on GAAP EBITDA $155,861M: `16.13 × 155,861 = $2,513,038M EV; equity = $2,420,587M; per share ≈ $222.60`
- EV/NTM EBIT: `26.76 × 103,833 = $2,778,550M EV; equity = 2,778,550 − 235,540 + 143,089 = $2,686,099M; per share = $247.02`
- P/NTM EPS: `31.01 × $8.37 = $259.56/share`

**The LTM EBITDA row has a dual basis problem.** At 16.13x on CIQ-adjusted EBITDA (~$172.7B) the implied price is ~$266; at 16.13x on GAAP EBITDA ($155.9B) it is ~$223. Because the CIQ band was constructed on CIQ's adjusted EBITDA basis, the consistent reversion is at ~$265–266, not $223. Both are shown for transparency.

**Base-case illustrative point (single named multiple, directional only):** the own-median EV/NTM EBITDA multiple of 12.98x applied to FY2026 consensus EBITDA of $211,027M implies approximately **$243 per share** — approximately +2% above the current price of $238.34. The dispersion across the four multiples used (median basis) spans $243–$266 using CIQ-adjusted EBITDA bases, or $223–$260 using GAAP EBITDA for the LTM row.

**Reversion assumption and its validity.** The implied-value table assumes that today's warranted multiple equals the 18-month own median — i.e., that the business has not changed in a way that justifies a permanently lower multiple. That assumption is partially supported: Amazon's revenue growth has accelerated and margins are at record highs (13.1% EBIT in Q1 2026 versus 5.3% in FY2021). The warranted multiple for a structurally higher-margin Amazon is plausibly at or above the 18-month median. What creates downside to the reversion thesis: (1) AI capex is compressing FCF and the market may re-rate the multiple lower if FCF does not recover by 2026–2027; (2) the 18-month window itself includes a period when the stock was trading at near-peak multiples (Dec 2024); the median is pulled upward by those prints.

---

## 5. Own-History Read

Over the 18 months of available CIQ multiple data, Amazon has de-rated by approximately 8–10% on forward earnings multiples (EV/NTM EBITDA and P/NTM EPS), sitting in the bottom quartile of its own short-range band. The directional reversion to the own median implies a stock in the range of $243–$260 on a single-point NTM basis — roughly in line with, or modestly above, the current price, depending on which multiple is applied.

The single biggest caveat is that the 18-month own-history band is too short to produce a reliable reversion target. Amazon has undergone a structural earnings inflection — EBIT margin tripled from 2022 to 2026 — that means its own pre-2024 multiples are not a valid comparator. The relevant multiple history is the current 18-month window, but that window itself spans only one full capex cycle and does not yet include a period of normalised FCF delivery (FCF is negative LTM on a strict basis). If FCF remains negative or weak through 2026–2027 as capex runs at $150B+ annually, the multiple the market assigns to AWS-driven earnings may remain compressed relative to the historical midpoint, and the 12.98x NTM EBITDA median may not be "the old normal" so much as a data artifact of a brief high-valuation period in late 2024. Reversion to that median is directionally informative but not a firm anchor.

## 2. Peer Multiples & Operating Stats
